activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
Aidan had told everyone he knew how to cook, which was true in the way that knowing the alphabet is knowing literature. His mother was working the late shift, his father was hopeless, and somewhere between the cereal aisle and the dairy case it had been agreed, mostly by him, that he would make Sunday dinner. A real one. The roast sat in his cart like a dare, pale and enormous in its plastic wrap, alongside potatoes he chose by knocking on them as though they owed him money.

"Planning a funeral or a feast?" Nancy fell into step beside him, having appeared the way she always did, out of some adjacent aisle and mild judgment. She picked up the meat thermometer he was scrutinizing and turned it over. "You don't own one of these."

"I own ambition," Aidan said. "That's basically the same thing."

Alejandro materialized behind them carrying a basket with, as far as anyone could tell, only hot sauce and a single lime in it. "I heard the word ambition and came running," he said. "Whose dinner is being ruined?"

The problem, though Aidan would not have phrased it as a problem until later, was the number. The recipe card, printed from the internet in the library like contraband, said 145 degrees, pull it at 145, and Aidan had taken this as scripture. He believed in recipes the way he believed in bus schedules: as things written by competent strangers who had thought about his situation personally. Nancy, holding the card at arm's length in the checkout line, was less convinced. "It says rest for fifteen minutes," she pointed out. "What do you think happens in fifteen minutes?"

"Resting," said Aidan, with dignity. "Meat gets tired."

"Meat is dead, Aidan."

"Then it's a very convincing performance."

Mr. Tan was ahead of them in the line, buying what appeared to be a week's worth of vegetables and nothing else, and he turned at this exchange with the polite torment of a man deciding whether to intervene. He taught chemistry at the school and lived, rumor held, entirely on stir-fry. He looked at the roast, then at the thermometer, then at Aidan's face, which was doing its confident thing. He opened his mouth, closed it, and paid for his vegetables. Whatever he knew, he was keeping, which Nancy found suspicious and Aidan found irrelevant.

Back in his kitchen, the roast went in at three o'clock sharp, and Aidan entered a state he would privately call vigilance and everyone else would call pacing. Alejandro showed up with the lime, claiming to have nothing else to do, and sat on the counter narrating. Nancy arrived second, ostensibly to make sure no one burned the house down, actually because her own house was quiet in a way she disliked. The three of them ate crackers and monitored the oven like NASA staff awaiting reentry.

At 144, Aidan pulled the pan out, triumphant, holding the thermometer aloft. The probe read 145 within a minute of sitting on the counter, and he wrote that off as momentum. Then it read 147. Alejandro leaned over his shoulder. "It's still going up. Is it supposed to do that?"

"It's resting," Aidan said, but the word had gone strange in his mouth. He watched the display climb with a somatic dread, an actual coldness in his hands, and somewhere in his head a door opened onto Mr. Tan's closed mouth in the checkout line. He looked it up, thumbing through his phone with the roast staring at him from the counter like an accomplice. Carryover cooking, the screen said. Food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests. Several. He said the phrase out loud, "carryover cooking," mostly to punish himself with its plainness.

"So you took it out at the target temperature," Nancy said slowly, assembling it, "and it's going to overshoot."

"I took it out at the finish line," Aidan said, "and it kept running."

They carved it anyway. The outside was beautiful, mahogany and crackling, and the inside was well done in the way that well done is a euphemism. Alejandro ate three slices and declared it a triumph of texture if not of moisture. Nancy ate hers thoughtfully and said it was good, which from her was practically a commendation. Aidan sat with his plate and his failure and, peculiarly, a rising good humor, because the evening had catalyzed something in him that success never did: the specific pleasure of having been wrong in a learnable way.

He understood, in a way he could not yet fully articulate, that two things he believed were both true and had been quietly at war. The recipe said 145 and the recipe was right. The roast would exceed 145 and that was also right, a fact with its own calm authority, and neither one contradicted the other; they simply required him to hold them together and subtract, next time, with some discernment about how much. How many degrees, exactly, several meant, he could not say, and he admitted this to the table.

"So next Sunday," Alejandro said, reaching for the last potato.

"Earlier," Aidan said, and got up to preheat the oven.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
story:
The community centre had one room with good light, the corner by the vending machines, and Parker claimed it every Tuesday at four because Mr. De Vries ran the homework club there and because the placement retake was on Friday. He had missed the cutoff by two marks. Two marks was the difference between starting calculus with Maina and Kelsey in September and sitting through a semester of precalc he had already, in every way that mattered to him, finished. Mr. De Vries had agreed to sign the retake slip only if Parker showed up all week, so Parker showed up, hunched over a workbook, a pencil going soft in his grip.

The problem was a polynomial, a long ugly thing, and the question asked for its maximum. Parker could differentiate it fine now; three days of drills had made the mechanics almost boring. What he could not see was how the derivative told him anything about a peak. He kept computing values, plugging in numbers on either side of the critical point, checking them against each other like a man measuring water with his hands.

"You're doing it the hard way," Maina said, dropping into the chair across from him with her own workbook, which she was not opening. Kelsey slid in beside her and immediately stole three of Parker's gum pieces, which was Kelsey's way of saying hello.

"There's a hard way and a wrong way and I've done both," Parker said.

Maina spun his worksheet to face her. She read the function, then the critical point Parker had circled, then looked at him with an expression he found faintly insulting. "You were at your grandpa's in the spring," she said. "You told me about the napkin."

He had almost forgotten telling her. The flashback arrived whole: his grandfather's kitchen, the smell of onions, his older cousin arguing that the biggest profit happened at the edge of some production curve, and Parker, who had wanted to preempt the whole argument, had said no. His grandfather had slid a napkin across the table and handed Parker the pen himself, which in that house was a kind of dare. On the napkin Parker had drawn a line across the critical point, tested a value before it and a value after it, and marked the results: positive, then negative. The cousin had gone quiet. By the first derivative test, Parker had said, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls. The cousin had looked at the napkin for a long moment and then laughed and poured him more juice, and the argument was over.

He had understood it that night as a thing that settled arguments. It had not occurred to him that it was a tool he was allowed to keep.

"Draw the chart," Maina said now, not gently. "Like on the napkin."

Parker took a fresh sheet and drew a number line. He marked the critical point. Left of it he tested a value and the derivative came out positive; right of it, negative. Positive to negative. The function rose and then fell. It was the shape of a hill, and he had been standing on this hill all week without recognizing it. He wrote "local max" beside the point and, for the first time all afternoon, felt the somatic relief of it, shoulders dropping, breath going long, the way his body relaxed before his mind agreed to.

"Wait," Kelsey said, mouth full of gum. "That's it? That's the whole thing you've been agonizing over? It's just, does it go up and then come down?"

"That's the whole thing," Parker said.

Mr. De Vries drifted past with his coffee and looked at the sign chart for perhaps two seconds. "Friday," he said, and moved on toward the chess boards near the window, where the late sun was coming in flat and grey as a steppe, all that open light with nothing rising in it.

Parker copied the method into the back of his notebook where he kept things he did not trust himself to remember. There was a second practice problem on the page and he solved it in four minutes, chart and all, though he noticed that he still could not have said, standing at a whiteboard with the retake proctor watching, whether he would reach for the chart or freeze. Some uncertainty he was honest enough to leave alone.

Maina leaned over and drew a small hill on the corner of his page, an arrow climbing its left side and an arrow skidding down its right, and wrote beneath it: up, then down.

"Keep it," she said. "For Friday."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
The mall closed at nine, and Eli had been standing near the fountain since eight twenty, rehearsing. He and Tenley had one hour and ten minutes, because her mother would be in the parking lot at nine thirty, no later, no negotiating, and in that hour they were supposed to see each other the way people who had agreed to a date saw each other. He had spent three days deciding on the shirt, and now that the hour had begun, the shirt felt like an auxiliary detail, a small supporting fact about him, while the main fact, that she had said yes at all, kept rearranging itself in his mind.

She came up the escalator with her jacket over one arm, and the first thing she said was, "I have to be at the north lot at nine thirty, so we should probably not start anything we can't finish." She meant the movie. The movie was ninety minutes, which neither of them had done the math on until that moment, and they stood there laughing at their own planning failure while the fountain hissed behind them.

They bought pretzels instead and walked the long loop past the shuttered jewelry counter and the store where Mr. Traoré sold phone cases and chargers. He had been kind to Eli all summer, letting him charge his dying phone behind the register, and he raised a hand now without leaving his conversation with a customer. Tenley talked about her sister leaving for school and how the house had gone quiet in a way nobody had predicted, and Eli noticed that she held her pretzel with both hands, tearing small pieces off, and he matched his pace to hers without deciding to.

Near the arcade, Kaylie was working the prize counter, folding receipt paper into tiny fans. She and Eli had been in the same health class in the spring, a semester of a teacher reading from slides while everyone privately memorized other things. "Hey," she said when she saw them, and then, because Kaylie had never once managed tact, "Oh, this is a date. Okay. Behave." Tenley raised an eyebrow, and Kaylie said, "That's all I'll say," and fanned herself with the receipt paper like someone who had said a great deal.

They played two games of air hockey, and between the second and third, Tenley said, "You can hold my hand if you want," and Eli, whose entire nervous system had been orbiting that possibility since eight twenty, did. It was warm and slightly pretzel-salted, and they walked the loop again, and it was good in the uncomplicated way he had suspected it might be, and he began to understand that some of the evening's happiness had been standing off to the side waiting for permission.

At nine fifteen the overhead speakers announced that the mall would close in fifteen minutes, and the ceiling lights dimmed by some preordained fraction. They headed for the north exit, past Mr. Traoré locking his gate, and Eli was already composing, in some back room of himself, the version of this walk he would tell his cousin tomorrow. He had wanted to instantiate everything he felt into one clean gesture, a hand squeeze at the door, something she could keep, and he was gathering his courage for it when Tenley stopped.

"Hey," she said. "So, the hand thing. I think I'd rather just say goodnight here." She said it without apology and without cruelty, the way you state a change in the weather. Eli felt the sentence arrive ahead of his understanding of it, and his first response, formed in half a second and then deliberately not spoken, was to ask why, which he recognized immediately as the wrong shape of question, the kind that treats a yes as a contract with fine print. Instead he let go, fully, fingers open, not a lingering version of letting go. "Okay," he said. "Goodnight."

"It was a really good night," she said. "I'm not being polite. I mean it." And then, because she was smarter than the average slide deck, she added, "You know you can do that, right? Say yes to something and then change your mind. Even after. Anytime, whenever. Kaylie drilled it into me sophomore year and it's the one thing I actually remember." She smiled. "You did it without making it weird. That's not nothing."

They walked out into the lot together anyway, handless, and the doors locked behind them with a sound like punctuation. Her mother's car was already there, headlights on, and Eli stood a step back while Tenley got in, and he raised a hand to her mother, who waved back with the brisk forgiveness of someone on a schedule. He watched the taillights cross the empty lot and merge onto the avenue, and he took out his phone to text his cousin that it had gone well, and stopped, because there was a text already waiting from Tenley, sent from the passenger seat: "Sunday? There's a ninety minute movie I want to actually finish this time."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal.
story:
The interregnum between the last day of exams and the first day of his summer job had lasted exactly one afternoon, and Jack was spending it in the back room of the corner store with his math textbook propped against a case of cola. Ms. Francis had agreed to pay him to restock shelves and count inventory, and she had also, in a moment he still did not understand, agreed to let him do his calculus review back there as long as he stopped when a customer needed the till.

The problem was money, which was to say the problem was that Jack was impecunious in a way that his part-time wages were not going to fix quickly enough. His mother had mentioned the transmission, once, in the tone she used for facts she wanted him to treat as weather. He had decided, without announcing it, to cover his own expenses for the coming year, and the calculus exam in August was the one thing standing between him and the scholarship that made the plan arithmetic rather than fantasy.

The page wanted him to find the maximum of a function, some curve that rose and then fell, and the textbook kept gesturing at an idea he could not quite hold still. He had drawn the graph three times, and each time the line seemed to undulate up and over like a hill on a road he had once biked in the rain, the top of it strangely flat when he actually got there.

The bell over the door rang. Ryley came in with Klara, both of them still carrying the smell of the pool, and found Jack in the back with the textbook and a calculator and a bag of cheese curds he had not yet scanned.

"You're doing math," Ryley said, "in a store. On the first day of freedom."

"I'm doing math in a store on the first day of being employed," Jack said. "There's a difference, and the difference is four dollars an hour."

Klara pulled a stool over and looked at the graph upside down. "That's the profit thing, isn't it. From the review sheet." She had done the same sheet, evidently, and survived it, because she was now rotating Jack's calculator in her hands with the calm of someone who had already been defeated and recovered.

"I keep trying the highest y-value I can guess," Jack said. "I plug in numbers and write them down and pick the biggest one. But the answer key says I'm close, not right."

"That's because you're hunting," Klara said. "You want the exact spot. Look at the top of your hill."

He looked. She put one finger on the curve at its peak and slid a pencil along it, flat, level, like a table. "At a local maximum of a polynomial," she said, "the derivative equals zero." She tapped the slope. "The tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal."

"So I take the derivative," Jack said slowly, "and I set it equal to zero, and I solve for x."

"You take the derivative and set it equal to zero and solve for x," Ryley repeated, in the voice of a man translating scripture, though Ryley had failed the same unit twice and was mostly there for the cheese curds.

Jack did it. The function was a polynomial, the derivative came out clean, and when he set it to zero the x fell out in two moves, and there it was, the exact coordinate of the peak. He checked it against his page of guessed values and found that his best guess had been beside the true point by a distance that was small and, he felt, insulting.

"There's something backward about it," he said, while Klara ate a curd and Ryley read the nutrition label like it owed him money. "I spent an hour trying every number I could think of, like the answer was hiding in a list somewhere. And the whole time the way in was the flattest part of the curve. The one place where nothing is happening."

"Nothing is happening at the top," Ryley agreed. "Which is why I don't plan to have a maximum."

The bell rang again. Ms. Francis came through from the front with a clipboard and the expression of a woman who had heard math being discussed in her stockroom and had decided to tolerate it. She looked at the graph, then at Jack, and asked him what it was for. He told her, a little stiffly, that it was the profit curve from a made-up business, the highest point being where you made the most money, and that you could find that point by taking the derivative and setting it to zero, because at the top the tangent line went flat.

Ms. Francis said, "Huh," and then said that the freezer aisle needed restocking before the evening rush, and that if the calculus could tell her which day of the week her ice cream sales peaked, she would consider raising his wage by a dollar.

Jack said he would need the numbers first. She said the numbers were in a ledger going back nine years and that they were a mess. Rylei said, "Guess every day and pick the biggest," and Klara threw a cheese curd at him, and Jack closed the textbook, took the clipboard, and walked toward the freezer with the pen behind his ear, already deciding he would do both, ledger and calculus, and see which one agreed with the ice cream.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.
story:
Jesse had told his mother he would handle dinner entirely on his own, a promise made with the flourish of someone who had watched exactly four cooking videos and felt, therefore, prepared. Now he stood at the folding table dragged into the backyard, a portable burner humming beside a bowl of marinated chicken, slicing a red onion while the last of the daylight went amber over the fence. He had planned a stir-fry with a peanut sauce, and he had planned it loudly, at school, where Daphnee had heard him and invited herself over, and where Elie had invited himself over on principle.

"You're doing the sauce by memory?" Daphnee asked, sitting cross-legged on the picnic blanket with a glass of lemonade she had poured without asking. Her want was simple and declared: she wanted the sauce to be restaurant-quality, because she'd had real peanut sauce at a place downtown once and had been chasing it ever since, a pursuit she described as "my whole personality this month."

"It's in my head," Jesse said. "Soy sauce, lime, peanut butter, a little honey, garlic. It's not complicated."

Elie, sprawled on the grass with Jesse's phone open to the recipe, cleared his throat in a way that suggested a lawyer about to enter evidence. "The recipe says two eggs, beaten, folded into the noodles at the end."

"There are eggs," Jesse said, with the confidence of a man who had not checked.

"There are eggs," Elie repeated, in the tone of a man about to check.

The problem revealed itself in stages, the way small disasters do. The recipe also wanted the eggs tempered with a ladle of hot sauce first, then stirred in off the heat, which meant Jesse needed them at the precise moment the noodles hit the pan, not ten minutes later. He had already lit the burner. The chicken was already searing, spitting pleasantly, filling the backyard with a smell that made the whole enterprise feel momentarily destined for success. Elie returned from the kitchen holding an empty egg carton the way one holds a verdict.

"Two eggs," Elie said. "Zero eggs in the house. The math is not munificent."

"That's not what munificent means," Daphnee said.

"It means generous, and the universe was stingy, so, close enough." Elie set the carton on the table like a trophy for the prosecution.

Jesse stood there with tongs in one hand and the awareness, arriving all at once, that he had started cooking before reading the recipe to the end. The neighbor's wind chime tinkled. The chicken needed flipping. Down the fence line, Mr. Bakker was watering his tomatoes in shorts and sandals, and Jesse, desperate, called across the divide between their two kingdoms.

"Mr. Bakker, do you have eggs?"

Mr. Bakker considered the request with the gravity of a border official. "I have eggs. What am I getting?"

This was the negotiation. Mr. Bakker, a man who believed no favor should travel unpaid, wanted recompense, and what he wanted was leftovers, since his daughter had stopped cooking for him since moving out and he was tired of toast. Jesse agreed to trade a full plate of the finished dish for two eggs, a rate Daphnee called extortionate and Elie called "the free market at work in its purest form, honestly beautiful." Mr. Bakker delivered the eggs over the fence in a ceramic bowl he wanted back.

The pause gave Jesse time to think, which was the thing he had been avoiding. He scrolled back through the recipe and saw, at the top, a note he'd skipped: prepare everything before you start. There was even a French phrase for it, which Elie read aloud with terrible pronunciation. "Mise en place," Elie announced. "It means putting in place, getting all your ingredients measured and ready before you cook."

"So it's not just being fancy," Jesse said. "It's a rule because of exactly this."

"Congratulations," Daphnee said. "You have discovered why every kitchen on earth is organized. Do you want a certificate?"

He wanted, if he was honest, both things at once: to feel that cooking was instinct, something he could do from the shoulder like an athlete, and to have the small, boring safety of having everything lined up in little bowls before the pan was hot. He couldn't have both, and he wasn't sure yet which one he actually wanted to be his. For tonight he chose the bowls. He sent Elie for the soy sauce, Daphnee for the lime, and he measured the peanut butter by eye, then, on reflection, by spoon, and cracked the two eggs into a cup and beat them while the chicken rested under foil.

The sauce came together glossy and sharp, the lime cutting the peanut butter's sweetness, and when Jesse folded the tempered egg into the noodles off the heat, it ribboned through them in pale gold threads. Daphnee tasted it, closed her eyes, and held up one finger for silence, which lasted four seconds.

"It's not the downtown place," she said. "It's mine now. I'm codifying this recipe. It goes in a notebook, with your name at the bottom in small letters."

They ate at the folding table as the sky went purple, and Jesse loaded a plate with the best-looking portion, set a fork on it, and carried it to the fence.

"Egg tax," he said, and handed it over.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, the first movement's recapitulation begins unusually in F major, the subdominant, instead of the home key of C major.
story:
The piano in the basement of St. Aldhelm's had been donated decades ago and smelled like it, and Clara had claimed it the way you claim an antiquated machine nobody else wants, by learning its one sticking key and its soft, buzzing E. She spread her photocopy of Mozart's K. 545 across the music stand and began drawing a bracket in pencil, then stopped. The church upstairs was quiet except for the sound of Mr. Grewal's vacuum moving along the aisles, back and forth, like breathing.

"You're marking the exposition already?" Naila asked from the folding chair where she sat with her own copy, unmarked, her chin on her fist. They had a theory exam in nine days, and Mr. Grewal, who kept the keys to the hall and had once been a school music teacher, let them rehearse down here on Thursdays if they stacked the chairs afterward.

"First theme, transition, second theme, closing bit," Clara said, pencilling labels. "Then the development starts here, and then the recapitulation begins..." She ran her finger along the staves and stopped again, because the notes under her finger were not doing what the notes were supposed to do. She had learned the rule plainly enough: when the first theme comes back, that is the recapitulation, and it comes back in the home key. The movement was in C major. C major was all over the first page like a stamp. But the return she was looking at sat on a flat, and she counted it twice. F major. She put the pencil down.

"Kaya would know," Naila said, and dug out her phone. She typed for a while, then turned the screen so Clara could read the message: "Ask her if she's found the first theme coming back yet. Tell her the trick is the key, not the tune. Don't tell her more than that or she'll sulk." Then a second bubble arrived: "Is she sulking?" Clara said she was not sulking, she was thinking, and Naila typed this back with a straight face, which felt, to Clara, like a small act of mendacity, since Clara's shoulders were up around her ears.

The vacuum had stopped. Footsteps came down the stairs, and Mr. Grewal appeared with a ring of keys in one hand. He looked at the two copies on the piano, at Clara's pencil hovering, and said nothing helpful, which was his way. He asked whether they had stacked the chairs. They had not. He said he would be upstairs another twenty minutes, and he climbed back toward the light of the nave, and the door swung shut behind him with its slow ecclesiastical sigh.

Naila watched Clara redraw her bracket three times, once at the return of the theme in F, once further on, once halfway between. Naila did not play piano herself; she sang, and had a habit of historicize ing pieces the way the exam workbook wanted, saying things like "in Mozart's time, audiences expected..." But she had listened to Clara play this movement so often that she could hum it entire, and now, watching Clara hesitate, she heard the movement in her head and noticed something Clara, squinting at print, could not. When the tune returned it did not land where her ear had been waiting for it to land. The home key arrived only later, quietly, almost apologetically. She hummed the moment out loud, then hummed where her ear had wanted it.

Clara went still. "Say that again." Naila hummed the return, then hummed the tonic chord, some distance after it, and Clara followed her finger down the page and found the second place, the C major, the actual resolution. So the bracket she had drawn was wrong, but not entirely wrong: the first theme really did come back where she had marked it. It came back in F major, the subdominant, instead of in the home key. Clara erased the bracket, wrote a small note in the margin, then sat on the piano bench with her hands in her lap. "Is it still the recapitulation," she said, "if it comes back in the wrong key? Or is it just, I don't know, a trick?"

"That's the kind of question the exam won't ask," Naila said.

"The exam asks where the recapitulation begins." Clara lifted the lid and set her hands over the opening bars. "Play it from there," Naila said, pointing at the return in F, and Clara played the theme in its strange borrowed light, both of them leaning toward the sound.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
The photo arrived during fourth period, and by lunch the whole grade was talking about it: a flooded underpass with a half-submerged car, captioned as the storm drain collapse on Miller Road, two blocks from school. Jazlyn had sent it to Emma with a string of exclamation points and a demand that Emma share it before the district covered it up. Emma sat in her mother's office after school, her mother having insisted she wait there until the five o'clock meeting ended, and she stared at the image on her phone with her thumb hovering over the share button. Something about the water looked wrong. Not wrong like a fake, exactly, but worn, the way a picture looks after it has circulated for years, cropped and recompressed until the edges went soft.

The deadline was real, in its small way. Jazlyn wanted a group post up before the evening news, before somebody else claimed the scoop, and the school paper's adviser had told Emma last week that being first mattered less than being right, a principle Emma had nodded at without feeling it in her hands. Now her hands felt it. She could post the photo and be part of the story, or she could wait and risk looking slow, or scared, or indifferent to a collapsed drain that might, on some version of the facts, actually threaten the kids who cut through that underpass to catch the bus.

"Rough day or math homework?" Mr. Nguyen asked from the neighboring cubicle. He was the office manager, a patient man who kept a jar of peppermints on his desk and had never once asked Emma to justify her presence among the filing cabinets.

"Trying to figure out if a picture is a lie," Emma said.

"Ah," he said, and rolled his chair back to his monitor, as though lying pictures were a category he had retired from.

Emma texted Yusuf, who was the kind of person who read the footnotes of things. He answered fast, which meant he was avoiding his own homework. "You can search a picture instead of words," he wrote. "Upload it to TinEye. It's a reverse image search engine, been around since 2008. Way older than you'd think."

She typed it in on her mother's spare laptop, the office one with the missing shift key, and uploaded the photo. The site said it could sort the results with the oldest first, and she clicked that option because the newest copies were just the day's panic multiplied, everybody reposting everybody. The oldest ones came up slow, then all at once: the same flooded underpass, the same unfortunate car, dated years before. Not Miller Road, and not this storm, and not anyone's breaking news. The picture had simply been waiting, patient as entropy in a drawer, until some storm gave it a job to do again.

She sat with that for a minute. It was strange to feel both relieved and foolish at the same time, and stranger still to feel a kind of respect for the photo, which had done nothing but exist while people supplied it with fresh emergencies. Jazlyn would not take it well. Jazlyn had already posted the photo herself, had already used the word "cover-up," and Emma understood the impulse better than she wanted to admit, because the impulse was partly hers. Wanting to be the one who told people, wanting the small aggrandizement of being first with the alarm, was not a motive she could pretend she'd never felt. She could only decide what to do with it now that she could see it.

She called Jazlyn instead of texting, because the incipient fight deserved a voice. "The picture's from years ago," she said. "I searched it backward. It's not Miller Road at all."

There was a silence long enough that Emma could hear the office's printer finishing a job somewhere down the hall. "Everyone already shared it, though," Jazlyn said finally. "Including the news account with the blue check."

"That doesn't make it true. That just makes it fast."

She walked Jazlyn through the search, step by step, her mother's spare laptop turned so the screen faced the window and the parking lot going amber. She admitted what she still didn't know, that the underpass might still flood, that a real warning could hide inside a fake photograph, that checking one lie wasn't the same as knowing the truth. When she hung up, Mr. Nguyen was holding out the peppermint jar.

"For the lying picture?" he asked.

"For the ones I almost told," Emma said, and took two.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.
story:
The quiz was Tuesday, and Katherine had promised Mr. Holloway she would retake it whether she was ready or not. "You wrote that RNA polymerase unwinds the DNA," he had said, handing back the page with its red slash across the top. "You're describing the wrong enzyme at the wrong moment. Come see me when you can walk me through it from the beginning." So on Thursday she stayed after the bell, along with Rafael, who had failed the same quiz for entirely different reasons, and Sonny, who had passed it and claimed to be there only for the company.

The lab smelled like the agar plates nobody had put away, faintly sweet and slightly off. Katherine set up the model kit on the long bench near the window: plastic base pairs in pastel colors, little pegs for the sugar-phosphate backbone. Mr. Holloway had gone to the supply closet, which meant they had ten minutes of unsupervised failure ahead of them.

"Start from the top," Rafael said. He was unzipping his jacket one tooth at a time, a habit he had when he was thinking, the sound like a small animal gnawing. "DNA gets copied. Then what."

"Then RNA gets made off it, then the RNA gets read by a ribosome, then you get protein. Transcription, translation. I know the order. I know the words." Katherine snapped two base pairs together, then took them apart again. "I just can't make it feel like a machine instead of a vocabulary list."

"It is a vocabulary list," Sonny said from the stool by the sink. He had his chin in his hand, doing his impression of a stoic, which mostly involved looking bored in a way he clearly practiced. "That's what biology is. A vocabulary list with diagrams."

"It's not." Katherine heard how shrill she sounded and lowered her voice. "Mr. Holloway said my problem is I memorized the names without the sequence. If I can't say what happens first, I don't actually know anything."

Rafael stopped at the third tooth of his zipper and held the jacket open, studying it. Then he turned it sideways so she could see the two halves hanging apart. "Okay. Watch. Before anything else happens, before anything can be copied, something has to open this up." He pulled the slider down the rest of the track in one motion and the jacket fell open like a book. "The enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix. It breaks the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together."

Katherine looked at the jacket, then at her model, where the paired pegs were held by nothing but friction. "Wait. The bonds between the bases. Not the backbone."

"That's what the book said," Rafael said, suddenly less certain. "Page 214. I read that page nine times because the quiz ate me alive."

"It's why it can unzip," Sonny said, straightening up, the stoic abandoned. "The backbone is covalent, it's the strong one, it runs the whole length. The bases in the middle just cling to each other. You pull those apart and the whole thing opens down the middle." He picked up the model, wrenched the paired pegs apart with his thumbs, and the double helix sagged open into two lopsided strands. "Like that. There's your helicase."

"That's what I got wrong." Katherine took the strands from him and held them apart, looking down the gap. "I had the enzyme cutting the wrong thing, so everything after it was in the wrong order. You can't copy anything until it's open, so helicase comes first, then the copying, then everything else." She laid the two strands flat on the bench, side by side, and started placing the little RNA pieces along one of them, matching bases. "This part is transcription. The RNA. Then it peels off and goes to the ribosome, and the ribosome reads it in threes and snaps amino acids together, and that's translation."

"And a protein walks out," Rafael said, zipping his jacket back up. "A protein with your hair color in it. Or your missing quiz answers."

Mr. Holloway came back with a stack of worksheets and found the three of them bent over the dismantled model. "Someone has been studying," he said, which in his mouth was practically a parade. "Miss Chen. Show me."

She talked for four minutes without stopping. She pointed at the open strands, then at the RNA she had laid down, then at the lumpy amino acid chain Sonny had snapped together out of the spare parts because he could not help himself. When she stumbled on the order of the ribosome steps, she paused, said "wait," and fixed it herself before anyone could jump in.

"Better," Mr. Holloway said. "The quiz is Tuesday. And Mr. Delgado, since you've clearly decided to learn the material after failing to learn the material, you may join her." He left the worksheets on the bench and went back to his desk at the front, where he sat with the particular stillness of a man pretending not to listen.

Rafael groaned. Sonny slid off his stool and started taking the model apart, sorting the pegs by color into the tray, which nobody had asked him to do and which Katherine suspected was his way of apologizing for the stoic act. "For the record," he said, "I was here for the company."

"You were here because you're disaffected and this room has better heating than the bus stop," Rafael said.

"Also that."

Katherine picked up one of the plastic base pairs, a little pink-and-yellow pair still clipped together, and turned it over. It was held by a single small tab, and she pressed it with her thumbnail until it popped apart, then clicked it back. She put it in her pocket with the loose change and the stub of pencil, and got out a fresh sheet of paper. "Okay," she said. "Again from the top. Quiz me."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: On a pyramid with five-year age groups, a bulge moves up one bar every five years, so today's large group of babies becomes a large group of schoolchildren soon after.
story:
The departure board flicked to DELAYED just as Madison found the gate, and she sat down between a man asleep against the window and a woman feeding coins into a vending machine that kept refusing them. In her lap sat the folder Ms. Ross had handed back that morning with a single line in red: good data, no argument. The geography presentation was due in thirty-six hours, and she was supposed to be on a plane to her grandmother's instead of in a classroom. She had told Ariel she would finish it on the way. She had told herself that, too.

Ariel dropped into the seat beside her with two coffees and the dour expression she reserved for airports. "Tony's getting the rental car sorted," she said. "He says we have three hours."

"Then I have three hours." Madison opened the folder. Inside was the population pyramid for the town where her grandmother lived, the one Ms. Ross had assigned almost as a joke, a small municipality nobody in the class had heard of before. The bars spread wide at the bottom, narrowed through the middle, thinned to almost nothing at the top. She had written four paragraphs describing it. Description, apparently, was not argument.

"What's the point of the thing, anyway?" Ariel asked, leaning over.

"You look at the shape and you decide what the place will need. More schools or more nursing homes. That's the whole question."

"And you don't know."

"If I knew I wouldn't be doing this." She said it more sharply than she meant to, and Ariel pulled back, sipping her coffee, watching the board.

Madison tried to force the pyramid into an answer. A wide base meant young people, so, schools, obviously. Except she kept remembering the town itself, the shuttered elementary wing her grandmother complained about, the senior centre with a waiting list. The town she knew and the diagram in front of her were telling two different stories, and one of them had to be wrong. She looked from the paper to the window, where a ground crew was pushing a luggage cart through the rain, and back again.

Tony arrived shaking water off his jacket. "Gate agent says weather in Denver. What are we fighting about?"

"Nothing," Madison said. "I'm trying to figure out when, not just what." She ran her finger up the side of the pyramid, counting the age bars. The bottom bar was the fattest, the one above it slightly smaller, and then a pinch, then a bulge again, her mother's generation. Her finger stopped. "Every bar is five years. So the whole shape slides up one bar every five years."

"Slides where?" Tony sat down across from her.

"Up. That fat bar at the bottom, all those babies, they're moving. Five years from now they're in the next bar up. So a big group of babies becomes a big group of schoolchildren soon after." She said it and then heard it, the way you sometimes only hear a thing once it's out of your mouth. "That's the answer. Not more schools now. More schools in five years, and whoever's building them should already be pouring concrete."

Ariel frowned. "But your grandma's town closed a school."

"Exactly. Because right now the town is old, the middle is hollow, and everyone's planning for nursing homes. But the bottom bar is huge, and it's climbing." Madison turned the folder sideways, then back, annoyed at herself for the theatre of it. She had been reading the pyramid as a photograph when it was a film. Ms. Ross wanted the argument in time, not in space.

"That's still a guess," Ariel said. "The babies could move away. Everybody moves away from that town. You did."

"It's a projection, not a prophecy." Madison wrote five years in the margin and then, underneath, probably, because she could feel the shape of the honest version now, the one that held both certainties at once. The bulge was real. The migration was real. Whichever force won would decide whether the town needed a new gymnasium or a new palliative wing, and she could not say which, only that the deadline for choosing was closer than anyone in that town believed. She thought of her grandmother's consciousness of the whole issue, how she tracked every birth announcement in the local paper while complaining that the streets were emptying. The old woman had been holding both facts at once for years without ever calling it geography.

"The last group's boarding," Tony said, standing, gathering his bag. He nodded at the folder. "So what are you going to tell them?"

Madison folded the pyramid so the fat bottom bar sat on top of the pinched middle, a shape that looked like nothing and predicted everything. "That the town has about five years to break ground on a school," she said, "and that I might be wrong."

"Confident." Ariel shouldered her backpack and got in line.

Madison followed her toward the jet bridge, still holding the folded paper against her chest like a boarding pass she hadn't been given yet.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
Justine locked the stall door, sat on the closed lid, and read the first card aloud under her breath, the way Mr. Demetriou had made them practise in the empty lab after school. Consent means someone can say yes, or say no, or change their mind after saying yes. She said it to the tile floor, then again to the metal divider, then once facing the stall door as if it were a row of seventh graders. Tomorrow she would stand in front of them for twenty minutes with these cards, and Mr. Demetriou had said the words had to come out steady, no apology in the voice, no trailing off.

The second card was harder. She turned it over twice before she could say it straight through: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. She'd underlined "typical," because the nurse at the training had tapped that word on the whiteboard like it was the hinge everything swung on. Justine said the sentence to the door again, and in the mirror-voice of the tiled room it sounded like someone else talking, someone competent, and she let herself enjoy that for a second.

Then the outer door banged and Keiran's voice came over the dividers, too loud the way he always was in bathrooms, like the acoustics owed him something. "Justine, tell my cousin he's an idiot. He says pulling out works fine, that the pill's basically a scam invented to make money." Justine stayed on the lid. "That's specious," she said. "It sounds like reasoning, but it isn't." She gave him the sentence off the card, slow, word for word, and heard him go quiet, which for Keiran was a kind of applause. "Seven out of a hundred," he repeated. "That's basically nobody." "That's basically seven whole people," she said. He flushed the tap, still arguing halfheartedly about his cousin, and left.

In the hallway outside, Henrik was waiting with his phone out, holding a place in the line for late buses. He'd promised to walk Justine partway home, mostly because he liked to argue with her, and he'd already worked out his opening move: he'd claim that the peer-health programme was just the school covering itself, liability dressed up as education. He texted her instead of knocking, because the door was heavy and the moment felt heavy too. u still in there? she'd been in that bathroom since the last bell.

The reply came in two bubbles. yes. tell mr d i'm not coming to practise tonight. Then, after a long minute: can you meet me at the clinic on Archer St at 4. Henrik stared at the screen. The clinic. He typed and deleted three jokes, which for him was unheard of, and finally sent only: i'll be there.

Inside the stall Justine put the cards away and did the thing she had been circling around all afternoon. She opened the app on her phone, the one with the small white pill icon, and scrolled back through the calendar of little grey checkmarks. June had a green check almost every day. July did not. There was a week at the lake, the week with the boy from summer whose name she had stopped saying even in her head, and in that week there were no checks at all, and then two checks, and then a gap of four days she couldn't account for except that she'd been staying at her grandmother's, where the evening routine dissolved into other people's routines. Her mother was on furlough from the plant and the household had gone loose at its edges, dinner at odd hours, everyone's habits drifting, and hers had drifted too. She counted the missed doses twice, both times arriving at the same ugly arithmetic, then closed the app and put her forehead against the cool metal door.

The fact from the card was not a card fact anymore. Seven in a hundred, with typical use, often because doses are missed, and she had been, it turned out, extremely typical. Mr. Demetriou thought she was nervous about presenting. Keiran thought she was hiding from his cousin's dumb opinions. Nobody had looked at her and seen the simpler, worse reason, which was almost funny, because the whole training had been about how you can't tell by looking.

The clinic smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazine. The nurse asked routine questions in a routine voice, and when Justine said she wanted testing for infections and a pregnancy test, the nurse just nodded and slid over a form, as if girls said this every hour, which apparently they did. While Justine waited she studied the contraception pamphlet, working out how she'd transliterate it for the seventh graders, turning "combined oral contraceptive" into "the pill, the one you take at the same time every day," turning "typical use" into "how it actually goes when people forget." At the counter the nurse pointed at a line on the form about reminders and asked, since Justine seemed to know the material, why she thought they pushed the daily phone alert so hard. "With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy," Justine said, "often because doses are missed." The nurse raised an eyebrow, half impressed, half something else, and said, "So you know that part." "I know it now," Justine said.

Henrik was in the waiting room with a car magazine he wasn't reading, and when the door with the little window opened he stood up before she was all the way through it. She had the paperwork folded into a square, the appointment card for next week, the little brown bag from the lab. She sat down beside him, took out the stack of flashcards, and clicked her pen. At the bottom of the second card, under the printed sentence, she wrote in small letters: say the part about forgetting. people forget. Then she put the cap back on the pen and handed the card to Henrik so he could hold it while she tied her shoe.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, which falls on April 4, 5 or 6, families visit their ancestors' graves to sweep and clean them and leave offerings of food.
story:
The gates of the cemetery went by on the left, and Gabriel's father drove past them without slowing, because the florist was another two hundred metres up the road and he wanted the flowers before the parking got bad. Gabriel sat in the back with his hands flat on his knees. In the footwell beside him sat a plastic bag with his grandfather's old folding knife in it, wrapped in a dish towel, because he had not been able to decide whether it belonged at the grave or at home in a drawer.

"We're only staying an hour," his mother said, turning around in the passenger seat. "Your uncle has to be back by three."

"An hour is fine," Gabriel said.

His phone buzzed. Jeremi had texted him a paragraph of sympathy that ended with a question about physics homework, which Gabriel understood was Jeremi's way of saying he did not know what else to say. Below that, an older message from Dave: *my family's at my grandpa's grave today too, we go every spring, same weekend as you basically.* Gabriel had read it four times since yesterday without answering.

The florist's van was parked half on the curb, its rear doors open, buckets of white chrysanthemums undulating gently in the draft from a fan propped in the doorway. His father went in. His mother stayed in the car and looked at the list of things still to do on her phone, and Gabriel, watching the shop's dusty window, found himself saying, "Dave's family does this every year. Goes to the grave, I mean. On a set weekend."

"Good for them," his mother said, not unkindly.

"They sweep it," Gabriel said. "Like actually sweep it, clean the stone. And they leave food. His grandpa's favourite dishes." He was assembling this from fragments, from things Dave had muttered over the years and one photograph he had once shown them of a grave with oranges and a little cup of tea on it, steamless and patient in the grass. "It's called Qingming. It falls on the fourth, fifth or sixth of April, that's why everyone goes the same weekend. That's why he said basically the same as us."

His mother lowered the phone. "We're a day early and we are not Chinese," she said, and then, softer, "but your grandfather would have liked the sweeping part. He liked a tidy grave." A sign taped to the florist's door said NO SOLICITING, and below it, in smaller print, that the cameras were a deterrence, though there were no cameras that Gabriel could see, only the fan turning its slow head.

His father came back with the chrysanthemums and a length of green weed cloth, and they drove to the gates, past them, up the narrow lane where the cedars made the light come down in bars. His uncle's car was already there, and his aunt was spraying something along the base of the stone, a noxious chemical smell that reached the car even with the windows up, so that Gabriel's father made a face and cracked the door to wave at his brother.

They stood around for a while. His aunt finished spraying. His uncle read the inscription out loud, though everyone knew it, and then everyone was quiet, and Gabriel understood that the visit had reached the point where it could end, that they could put down the flowers, get back in the car, and drive to the restaurant that had been booked, and that this was what was going to happen unless someone made it not happen.

"There's a broom in the shed by the taps," he said.

His uncle looked at him. "What?"

"There's a shed, by the taps, I saw it when we came in. I want to sweep the stone before we go." He could hear how it sounded, and he kept going anyway. "Not for any reason. It's dirty. There's moss on the letters."

His father glanced at his mother, and something passed between them that Gabriel could not fully read, and then his father said, "I'll come with you," and his aunt said she would put the cloth down while they did that. So Gabriel went to the shed and came back with a stiff push broom and a smaller hand brush, and he swept the ledge of the grave first, slow strokes, grit and last autumn's leaves gathering at the corner where he could pick them up with his hand. Then he knelt and worked the small brush across the carved letters of his grandfather's name, one at a time, the way Dave had described once, the way Gabriel had asked him about without knowing why he was asking.

"Hand me the cloth," his father said, and they lined the border together, and his aunt took a photograph of the finished grave with the chrysanthemums in front of it, and nobody said the word Qingming again or any other word about what it was or was not. His uncle looked at his watch and did not say anything about the time.

In the car afterward, his mother turned around before his father started the engine. "You never answered Dave," she said.

"I know." Gabriel typed while the cedars slid past the windows, bars of light and shadow crossing his hands. He wrote, *we went today too, we swept it, first time, my idea.* He looked at it, and after a second he added, *next year same weekend?* and pressed send, and put the phone face down on his knee as the gates came up ahead, open, and the car passed through them onto the ordinary road.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: In 2025, US union members had median weekly earnings of $1,404, compared with $1,174 for workers who were not union members, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
story:
Christopher stacked the last of the cereal boxes and checked his phone. Two hours left on his Saturday shift, and his feet had gone numb somewhere around noon. He was sixteen, three months into his first job at Fernbrook Market, and he had plans for the money: a laptop for college applications, maybe a bus pass so he didn't have to bike in the rain. At twelve dollars an hour, the laptop lived about five months away.

At the register, Eshal was arguing with the schedule taped beside the time clock. "They've got me closing Sunday and opening Monday," she said. "Nine p.m. to seven a.m. between shifts. I told the manager I have a chemistry final and he said, and I quote, we all make sacrifices." She tore the paper off the wall, looked at it, and put it back, as if the act of ripping it would cost her the job.

Christopher mopped near the doors while she vented. He wanted to say something useful, but all he had was sympathy, and sympathy didn't change a schedule. When his break came, he sat on the curb outside with a soda and called Isaac, who worked at Halden's, the grocery across town.

"You got your paycheck yet?" Isaac asked, before Christopher even said hello. "Because mine was three-fifty more an hour than yours. I did the math. And I work fewer hours, and I get a real break that's actually on the clock."

Christopher sat up straighter. "How? Halden's is the same kind of store. Same aisles, same everything."

"Our store's unionized. Yours isn't. We pay dues, but there's a contract. That's why the hours are set, the breaks are set." Isaac paused, and Christopher could hear him grinning. "Also, get this. I looked it up for a civics thing. In 2025, union members had median weekly earnings of one thousand four hundred four dollars, compared with eleven seventy-four for workers who weren't union members. Bureau of Labor Statistics."

"Say that again," Christopher said, and wrote the numbers on the back of his receipt with the moisture from the soda can. He'd been proud of his job, proud in a quiet way, the way he imagined his grandfather had been proud of thirty years at the plant. Now the pride had a comparison attached to it, and the comparison stung.

He flashed back to his interview in April, the office smelling of burnt coffee, the manager saying they were a family here and that hard work got noticed. Christopher had been so enraptrured by the idea of his own money that he hadn't asked a single question about wages or breaks or how schedules got made. He'd signed the paper while the manager watched, and the pen had skipped, and he'd initialed the smudge anyway.

Inside, Eshal was back at the register, scanning groceries with a sardonic little commentary under her breath, "Welcome to Fernbrook, where we all make sacrifices, would you like paper or plastic." Christopher laughed, then stopped laughing. He thought about sentience in robots, which they'd debated in Ms. Siddiqui's class, whether a machine that could feel discomfort ought to have rules protecting it, and he thought it was strange that humans had to argue the same thing about themselves. Rules, someone to negotiate them, someone to notice.

"I'm going to ask about the scheduling policy," he told Eshal. "In writing. Not because I think they'll change it, but because I want to see what they say when it's not just me complaining in the break room." He wasn't sure it would work. Maybe the answer would be no, maybe it would be nothing, maybe asking would make things awkward for months. He only knew that the numbers on his receipt felt like something he was allowed to carry into that conversation, and that Isaac's store existed, across town, proving it could be otherwise.

He punched back in, hung the mop on its hook, and walked toward the office door with the receipt folded small in his fist. Eshal watched him go. He knocked twice, and heard the manager say, "Come in."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index, published since 2002, scores 180 countries and counts concentration of media ownership as one pressure on press freedom.
story:
The argument started over the remote. Jeremy's father had the volume up on the evening bulletin, the anchor's voice filling the living room the way it did every night at six, and Jeremy wanted to switch to the coverage of the factory strike two channels over. "Same news," his father said, not looking up from his plate. "It's not the same news," Jeremy said. "The other one has people from the picket line on camera. This one has the company spokesman." His father waved the fork as if shooing a fly, and Jeremy sat down on the arm of the couch, defeated for the moment but not willing to let go of it.

He had noticed it a week ago, and it had bothered him since. Two channels, one story, and the difference between them was not the facts but the gravity, the order, the faces they chose. He pulled out his phone and texted Ivy, who was the sort of person who kept screenshots of things other people scrolled past. Do all these channels belong to the same company? he typed. She replied with a laughing emoji and then, a minute later, a link.

At the door twenty minutes later, Ivy arrived with Augustin, who brought chips and the confidence of someone who had already formed an opinion about everything. Mr. Ngo from next door was already there, having come over to return a ladder, and he settled into the corner chair when Jeremy's father offered tea and the conversation, apparently, was going to be public. "You're watching the one owned by the shipping family," Mr. Ngo said mildly, nodding at the screen. "The strike coverage got friendlier after they bought it." Jeremy's father frowned. "A paper's a paper. News is news."

"It feels axiomatic," Augustin said through a mouthful of chips, "that the news is just the news. Like, obviously. But that's exactly the thing to be suspicious of." Ivy had already opened her laptop on the coffee table, pushing aside the remotes and a stack of unopened mail, including a remittance slip from Jeremy's uncle abroad that nobody had dealt with yet. "Okay," she said, typing. "Let me check the actual ranking. Reporters Without Borders does a World Press Freedom Index. It's been published since 2002, and it scores a hundred and eighty countries." The screen filled with a list of names and numbers.

She scrolled, and the room leaned in without meaning to. "And one of the pressures on press freedom it counts," she went on, "is concentration of media ownership. So it's not just censorship, it's who owns the outlets." She found the country, read the number aloud, and read the short explanation beneath it, then sat back. Jeremy's father came around the couch, plate abandoned, and read it himself. "A hundred and eighty countries," he said slowly, "and this thing thinks it can score them all."

"Scores," Ivy corrected. "That's the verb they use."

The conversation loosened after that. Mr. Ngo talked about the papers of his youth, how each one had a flavor you could taste, and how readers learned to read around it the way you drive around a pothole. Augustin argued that knowing an outlet's owner should emancipate you from its framing, and Jeremy said he wasn't sure it was that clean. "You can know it and still be moved by it," he said. "The music, the anchor's voice, the little flag in the corner. Knowing who pays for the show doesn't turn the show off." Ivy pointed at him. "That's the most honest thing anyone's said tonight."

They stayed in the living room until the second bulletin came on, and Jeremy, mostly to see what would happen, suggested they watch the same story on both channels back to back. His father, to everyone's surprise, worked the remote himself, flipping between them with the concentration of a man refereeing a match. The first channel gave the strike ninety seconds and the spokesman the last word. The second gave it four minutes and ended on a woman in a hard hat saying she'd be back on the line at dawn. Nobody said anything for a moment, and the silence did the work.

"So what do we do," Augustin asked, "read everything twice?" "Read it twice from different owners," Jeremy said. "And admit we still won't be sure." His father turned off the television and stood there holding the remote, looking at the dark screen the way you look at someone who has just corrected you. "Tomorrow," he said at last, "we're watching the second one first." Then he pointed the dead remote at the set and pressed the button again, twice, out of habit, before he realized what he was doing.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
story:
The food bank smelled of cardboard and cold concrete, with something sweet underneath, like apples left in a crate too long. Alexandra pulled the hairnet lower over her ears and waited for someone to tell her what to do.

"You're the new one," said a boy in a green apron, sliding a box toward her across the long steel table. "I'm Nathaniel. Sorting. Canned stuff in the good bin, dented or swollen ones in the trash, and anything past its date goes in there too." He pointed to a blue tub with a torn label stuck on it that read DISCARD.

Alexandra sat down and began. Beans, tomatoes, soup, beans again. It was almost soothing, the small decisions, until she picked up a can of peaches, turned it over, and stopped. The date on the bottom had passed. Eight days ago. She held it a moment longer, its weight ordinary and its meaning suddenly unclear, then dropped it into the blue tub. Then another. A tin of sardines, a canister of oats. The tub began to fill, and something about the pile of it bothered her, though she could not yet say what.

"I'd slow down on that," said a girl across the table, without looking up. She had a laminated sheet pinned beside her elbow. "Alaa. I did your job my first Saturday and threw out half a shelf before Mr. Whitaker caught me."

"Caught you doing what they told me to do?"

"The date's a best before date," Alaa said. "It marks when the quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe. Sealed food past it may still be safe." She tapped the laminated sheet. "It's all on here. Most people don't read it. I didn't."

Alexandra looked into the blue tub. The peaches sat on top, their label bright, the fruit inside probably fine, probably sweet. She thought of her grandmother, who had kept a jar of expired things in her cupboard as a kind of principle, and of her mother, who threw out milk the day before its date on principle too, and how both of them had been certain. She had always assumed one of them was simply wrong. Now she understood it was less tidy than that. The peaches were probably fine. Probably. She lifted them out and set them back on the table, and her hand hovered there.

"So I just put them in the good bin? Even though the date's passed?"

Alaa shrugged. "Up to you. Some people still won't take them. Some of the folks coming through don't care, and some do. There's a subtlety to it. That's the part nobody tells you about volunteering, by the way. You make judgments all day and most of them are yours alone."

Mr. Whitaker came by with a trolley of bread. He was older, with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair, and he paused when he saw the peaches in Alexandra's hand. "Found the sheet, did you? Good. When people ask, I let them decide themselves. A person choosing their own can is different from a person being handed one."

"But how do I know when it's actually bad?" Alexandra asked.

He didn't launch into a lecture, though she could see he wanted to; she had watched teachers expatiate on this exact kind of question before, and his restraint was its own kind of answer. "Swollen, leaking, dented deep at the seam," he said. "Those go. The date alone, no." Then he wheeled the bread away toward the shelves, leaving her with the can.

She sorted for another hour. Most of what she pulled she kept; two swollen tins she threw out without hesitation, the decision suddenly easy when the can itself told her. When Nathaniel dropped a whole tray of pasta near her and swore under his breath, she helped him gather it, and he thanked her with a bread roll from the day-old rack, still soft in the middle.

Near closing, a woman came through the line with a little boy who clung to her coat. Alexandra was bagging now, and she reached for the peaches. She hesitated, then held the can where the woman could see the bottom of it. "The date's just past," she said. "It's about quality, not safety, sealed like this. But it's your call."

The woman turned it over twice, reading. "Peaches," the boy said, tugging the coat. She put the can in her bag, and her son smiled up at the bag like it was Christmas morning. "Thank you," she said. "Nobody ever tells you the whole thing."

"No," Alexandra said. "They don't." She reached for the next bag and started filling it.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: English newspaper headlines often drop small words like 'the' and use the present tense for past events, a compressed style sometimes called 'headlinese'.
story:
The newspaper arrived at Grandmother's house the way it had for forty years, thumped onto the porch before seven, and Annabelle was the only one awake to fetch it, which was how the whole thing began. She had been in the country for six weeks. Her aunt thought she should practice English with the paper because the paper was free and because her cousin Cole, who was supposed to tutor her, kept canceling. So every morning Annabelle sat at the kitchen table with a cold bowl of porridge and the front section, reading aloud to Grandmother, who could not hear well but pretended to listen with her whole face.

The article that morning was short, six paragraphs, about a library losing its funding. That was the assignment Mr. Wu had given her before school let out: one article, read it, then summarize it aloud without looking. "Summarize," he had said, "not translate. Translation is a cage. Summary is a door." She had written both sentences in her notebook because she liked them, though she did not entirely believe the second one.

The trouble was the headline. It said: COUNCIL CUTS LIBRARY BUDGET, PROTEST GROWS. She stared at it for a long time. In her own language, a sentence like that would need its small words the way a body needs its joints, and it would need its past tense, because the cutting had already happened, last Tuesday, at a meeting she read about in the third paragraph. Here there was no "the," no "has," no sign that anything was finished. It looked, to her, like a sentence that had been struck by lightning. "Council cuts library budget," she said to Grandmother. "This is not grammar. This is a crime scene."

Grandmother laughed her rattling laugh and turned up her hearing aid, which mostly amplified the kettle. Annabelle tried again, slower, hunting for the verb the way she used to hunt for shells on the beach near her old house. Then it landed, all at once, and she sat back in the chair. The small words were missing on purpose. The present tense was standing in for the past, like an actor playing a dead king. It was compressed the way her mother compressed leftovers into a container too small, everything pushed down to fit. She remembered Mr. Wu saying it once, weeks ago, when she'd half been listening, and now the word surfaced whole. "Headlinese," she said out loud. "He called it headlinese." Grandmother nodded as though this were a diagnosis she had suspected for years.

The summary was still ahead of her. She flipped the article face down, breathed, and began. "The council," she said, and was absurdly pleased to be using the word "the" again, like putting on a coat in a warm house. "The council cut the money for the town library. The people who use the library are angry. A protest, one hundred persons, happened on Saturday." Grandmother raised one hand. "Persons," she said. "People, dear. Persons is what you say when you're about to disenfranchise them." Annabelle wrote that down too. She did not think it was a real rule, but she liked the shape of it, the way it suggested that English kept its coldest words for its coldest purposes.

Cole showed up at noon, which surprised everyone, including possibly Cole. He had a biology textbook under his arm because he had nowhere else to put it, and when Annabelle told him about the headline he got excited in the way he got excited about things nobody else cared about. "That's like a whole phylum of writing," he said, dropping into the porch chair. "Headlines, telegrams, the tags on plants at the garden center. Compressed language. Its own branch of the tree." Annabelle said that was a beautiful way to make an ugly thing sound scientific, and he looked so briefly wounded that she softened and let him have the point. He quizzed her then, holding the paper above his head like a camp counselor. "Mayor defends plan," he read. "When did the mayor defend the plan?" "Already," she said. "Yesterday, probably. It just looks like now." He lowered the paper an inch, impressed.

But when she tried to say what she actually thought about the library, everything jammed. She wanted to say that a library losing money was not only a local matter, that in her own country her mother had signed petitions about exactly this, that books were the one thing that had never disenfranchised her even when everything else did. In English the sentence came out flat and small. "It is bad," she said, and heard how petulant it sounded, like a child denied a biscuit, and hated the language for a second, then hated herself for hating it, because the language had done nothing. It was just standing there, holding its arms out, waiting for her to bring it more.

Grandmother, who had followed none of the English and all of the feeling, patted the table and went to the cupboard. She came back with a tin of lemon drops so old the lid had to be persuaded, and set one in front of each of them. Then she pointed at the paper, at Annabelle, and held up one finger: again.

Annabelle turned the article over. Six paragraphs, one hundred angry persons, a headline like a struck match. She would get the summary right today and wrong again tomorrow; the door Mr. Wu had promised was also, she was beginning to suspect, a wall you could lean against and call a door. She put the lemon drop in her cheek, where it clicked against her teeth while she thought. "The council cut the money," she began, and Grandmother leaned in, hand cupped to her good ear.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: A 2002 study led by Richard Seager argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explain most of Europe's mild winters.
story:
The ocean current map covered the whole back wall of the climate gallery, blue rivers twisting across the Atlantic like spilled ink. Grace stood in front of it with her notebook open, copying the arrow that ran from the Gulf of Mexico up past Newfoundland and toward the British Isles. Her report for Mr. Cho's class was due in six days, and her thesis, printed neatly at the top of the page, read: The Gulf Stream warms northern Europe.

"You're doing the warm river thing too?" Arlo came up beside her, hands in his jacket pockets. "Quincy's doing sharks. Smart. Nobody argues with sharks."

"Nobody argues with the Gulf Stream either," Grace said. "It carries warm water north. End of story."

Arlo tilted his head at the map. "My cousin did a paper on it at college. She said there was some fight about it."

Grace wrote faster, as though the pen could settle the matter. "What kind of fight?"

"Some scientist said the story everybody tells is wrong. I don't remember his name. Seager, maybe."

She closed the notebook halfway, then opened it again. Mr. Cho had told them, on the first day of the unit, that a claim you couldn't defend against one counterexample wasn't a claim, it was a habit. She had liked that. She liked it less now.

They found Mr. Cho twenty minutes later in the weather room, watching a tank of dyed water rotate on a turntable. Grace showed him her thesis sentence. He read it, folded the page back, and handed it over without a word, which was the closest he ever came to telling a student she was wrong.

"The museum library has journals," he said. "Second floor. Ask the docent for the atmospheric science shelf."

The study was there, in a 2002 issue, and the name on it was Richard Seager. Grace sat at a carrel with the volume open while Arlo leaned over her shoulder, reading faster than she did. The paper argued that winds and the ocean's storage of heat through the seasons, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explained most of Europe's mild winters. Not a small correction. Not a footnote. Most.

"So the map is a travesty," Arlo said, pointing back toward the gallery. "The whole wall. They should take it down."

"It's not a travesty. The current is real." Grace tapped the page. "It's right there in the title, even. It's just not the whole answer."

"You sound like you're on both sides."
