She turned in the chair to face him. "I'm on the side of the thing that's true, which is apparently that Europe is mild for more than one reason. The Gulf Stream helps. The winds do more than people think. The ocean stores heat in summer and lets it out in winter. I can say all three."

Arlo wandered to the window while she photocopied the abstract. Below them, a school group was filing past the current map, and a docent was raising her arm toward the blue arrow, saying something they couldn't hear. Grace watched the kids' heads tilt up in unison.

From Arlo's place at the window, the group below looked like weather moving through the gallery, mercurial, surging toward one exhibit and then another. He could see Grace at the copier, feeding it coins, and he understood that she would spend the rest of the afternoon transmuting her neat one-line thesis into something longer and stranger and harder to present. He felt a small relief that it wasn't his report, and then a smaller, opposite feeling that he would rather hear hers than give his own.

At the carrel again, Grace drafted a new opening. The wind patterns over the North Atlantic, she wrote, and stopped. She crossed it out. Start with the old story, she decided, the one in every textbook, and then the study, and then what no one had fully settled. She read the Seager abstract twice more, looking for a sentence that said exactly how much of the mildness was winds and how much was the current, and there wasn't one, and she underlined that absence too.

Mr. Cho found them at closing time, standing at the wall map one last time. "Verdict?" he asked.

"The wall's not wrong," Grace said. "It's just quiet."

He looked at the blue arrow running north. "And your report?"

"Longer than it was this morning." She held up her notebook, where the old thesis line now had a single line through it, still legible underneath. "I'm keeping both versions visible. The class should see how it changed."

"That's the assignment," Mr. Cho said. "The rest was scaffolding."

Arlo pushed open the door to the lobby, and the evening air came in cold, and Grace pulled her jacket on. On the walk to the bus stop she tried the explanation out loud, twice, once for Arlo and once for no one, the winds, the stored heat, the current that helped but did not act alone, and when the bus arrived she was still saying, "Most, not all. That's the word I keep landing on. Most."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The dependency ratio compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, estimating how many dependents each working-age person supports.
story:
Madeline had the atlas open across her knees before Ms. Sutton's car cleared the county line, the population pyramids photocopied from the library running in a neat column down the page. Japan, narrow at the base and bulging near the top. Niger, a genuine pyramid, wide and young. Preston took up most of the back seat beside her, and Elise rode up front navigating, though the highway ran straight north for another four hours through boreal forest that showed no interest in turning.

"Quiz me," Madeline said.

"You're quizzing yourself. That's the whole point of this."

"Quiz me anyway. Ms. Sutton, is it the shape of the base or the shape of the middle that tells you about the workforce?"

Ms. Sutton kept her eyes on the road. "You tell me."

Preston leaned over the atlas, close enough that she could hear him breathing. "It's obvious. Old people everywhere, that's good news for taxes. Fewer kids means fewer schools to pay for. They shut a school in my cousin's town and everyone's taxes went down."

Madeline looked at the pyramid for Sweden, the base pinched, the 65-and-over bars stretching wide. "You're only counting one side of it," she said.

"There's two sides?"

"There's two kinds of people who don't work. Kids and old people. Both of them cost somebody something."

Her phone buzzed against her hip. Her father's name, and beside it the photo of the two of them at the lake. She hesitated, then answered, and Preston immediately turned away to the window as if granting her privacy in a car where none was possible.

"Madeline, I'm doing the budget tonight," her father said. "Property taxes came. They went up again, and I want to know who to be angry at. You're the geography person now. Isn't half the country too old to be paying for anything?"

She enunciated carefully, the way she did when she could tell he was dividing his attention between her voice and a spreadsheet. "It's called the dependency ratio," she said. "It compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64. It estimates how many dependents each working-age person supports."

There was a silence on the line long enough for a whole column of numbers. "So more old people means..."

"Each working-age person is supporting more people. If there aren't enough people between 15 and 64, the ones who are have to carry more. That's where your taxes come in. It's not just kids needing schools. It's nursing homes too. The ratio counts both ends."

"And you learned this from a pyramid."

"A population pyramid. It's a graph."

"Fine. When you're back, explain why my road tax paid for the road and it's still full of holes." He hung up before she could answer, which she recognized as his version of conceding a point. Preston was watching her in the visor mirror.

"So it's the whole shape," he said. "Not just the base."

"Not just the base."

They stopped for gas outside a town whose sign advertised a curling rink and a church, nothing else. Ms. Sutton handed Elise the club's cash box and reminded her, not for the first time, that as treasurer Elise had a fiduciary duty to count the change before they left the counter, and Elise counted it twice at the pump while Preston went in for sandwiches and came out with a bag of candy he had not been authorized to purchase.

From the moment the car door shut behind Preston, Elise kept her eyes on the receipt in her hand, though the arithmetic was done and correct. She had watched Madeline all morning, the atlas, the phone call, the way Madeline's thumb moved up the Swedish pyramid as she talked, tracing the bars like she was reading a person's face. Elise had known Madeline since seventh grade and knew the difference between her performing knowledge and actually holding it, and this morning it was the second thing, which was rarer.

The car was quiet when they pulled back onto the highway. Madeline had laid two pyramids side by side, Japan and Niger, and was writing in the margin, and when Elise leaned back to see, Madeline had written the same word on both pages and crossed it out on both pages.

"It doesn't work like I thought," Madeline said, not looking up. "I wanted a rule. Young country, build schools. Old country, build nursing homes. Done." She tapped Niger's wide base. "But look. Tons of kids, hardly anyone in the middle. Their ratio is terrible too. It's not old versus young. It's balanced or not balanced." She turned the atlas toward Elise. "Preston thinks aging means cheap. My dad thinks aging means robbery. They're both asking who pays, and the ratio doesn't answer that. It just says how heavy the load is. Who actually pays, how much, whether it's fair, that's politics. The graph can't tell us."

"So what do you write for the competition?"

"I write that Japan needs nursing homes and Niger needs schools, and then I write that both of them have too few people in the middle, and then I stop pretending I know what either country should do about it."

Preston unwrapped his sandwich. "So you're saying I was wrong."

"You were half wrong. There's a difference."

"And your dad?"

"Also half wrong. He just won't enjoy hearing it."

The trees closed back over the road, dark and even, and Elise folded the receipt into the cash box. Ahead of them the highway ran north, straight through the green, and Ms. Sutton reached over and turned down the radio without asking anyone.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Maria had claimed the table by the window on the second floor of the library, where the makerspace kept its kiln behind a folding partition, and she spread her pieces across the newspaper: six small bowls, thin-lipped, still damp enough to show her thumbprints. She had spent three Saturdays on them. Ronan dropped into the chair across from her and set down a single white vase, tall and narrow, with a celadon glaze he had mixed himself from a recipe he refused to share.

"You're loading today?" he asked. Mr. Rodríguez, who ran the space on weekends, had told them the kiln would run Sunday afternoon, and whoever wanted a spot had to have work bisqued and ready by closing. Maria said she was, and Ronan slid his vase toward the middle of the table as if the matter were settled, the way he did with most matters. She remembered then the bowl she had lost last spring, the one she had glazed in Esteban's copper green and fired alongside a piece of his that came out with her color bleeding into it, and how she had told herself it was the kiln's fault, the gods of the kiln, though she had known even then that she was really blaming her own carelessness about schedules.

At the kiln she found the clipboard Mr. Rodríguez kept on a nail, a firing chart someone had photocopied from a ceramics handbook and taped inside the lid of the supply box. She read it twice. Earthenware is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, the chart said, while porcelain goes in between about 1,200 and 1,400. She looked at her bowls, then at Ronan's vase, and understood at once that the two of them had been planning on a single load as though the kiln were a suitcase you could cram.

"Mine has to go low," she said, holding the chart out to him. "Yours has to go high. It's the same kiln, but it can't be the same firing." Ronan took the paper, read it, and did the thing she both liked and resented in him, which was to concede without appearing to. "So we amortize the cost of the run across two firings," he said, meaning they'd each pay half of both, or he'd pay more of one, and she noticed he'd already worked out which half he owed her. It was generous and it was also a way of deciding, quickly, so that nothing had to be argued through.

Esteban arrived with his backpack and no ceramics at all, only a chemistry textbook and the look of someone who intended to study near the kiln's warmth because his apartment was cold. When Maria explained the split, he tilted his head at Ronan's vase. "So it's porcelain. That's why it's so white." He asked whether porcelain was better, and Maria started to say no, then started to say yes, then stopped, because the honest answer was that porcelain was harder and finer and her earthenware was softer and warmer in the hand, and she could not rank them without pretending to a certainty she did not have. That was casuistry, her grandmother's word for arguing your way to whatever you already wanted, and Maria caught herself doing it in miniature and shut her mouth.

Ronan watched her hesitate and seemed, for once, to wait. He was not recalcitrant exactly; he could be persuaded, he simply made you do the persuading. "We could run yours Sunday and mine next Saturday," she said. "Or the other way." He said Saturday for his, since his glaze needed the longer soak anyway, and she agreed, and the arrangement was so ordinary that she almost missed what it cost her: the Saturday she had planned to give to her mother's yard sale, spent instead in this basement watching a kiln climb past 1,200 degrees and out of her clay's country.

She wrapped her bowls in the newspaper and carried them to the shelf Mr. Rodríguez had marked with blue tape, LOW FIRE ONLY, and there she set them in a row, thumbprints inward, where she could not see them and think about them. Last spring, when the glaze had bled, she had said nothing to Esteban for a week and then apologized with a muffin, and he had accepted the muffin and never mentioned the bowl again, which she had taken for forgiveness and was not sure now had ever required it.

Mr. Rodríguez came by at closing with his keys already out. "Two loads next weekend, then," he said, reading the clipboard, and Maria nodded. Ronan stood at the partition with his vase still in his hands, turning it so the celadon caught the fluorescent light, and Esteban had fallen asleep on his chemistry book, one hand curled around his pen.

"We could still fire everything together," Ronan said. "If we split the difference."

"Eleven hundred?" Maria said. "Your porcelain would never vitrify."

He smiled at the word and set the vase on the shelf beside her bowls, the white and the terra cotta standing apart under the blue tape, and turned off the light.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The U-Haul trailer thumped over every seam in the highway, a querulous rhythm Mason could feel through the seat, and his father kept adjusting the mirror as though the problem were the trailer and not the six hundred miles still ahead of them. Mason had his phone in his lap, screen dark, and he was not reading the message from Kaiya because he had already read it four times at the last gas station.

"You could say something back," his father said.

"In a while."

The message had arrived at 6:40 that morning, before anyone had loaded the last box. It said: I know you said goodbyes are pointless but I'm doing one anyway. Senior year is going to be wrong without you arguing with Mackenzie about whether sincerity is a performance. That's it. That's the whole letter. You better answer. Mason had started three replies in the driveway and deleted each one, because everything he drafted sounded either casual in a way he wasn't or heavy in a way he refused to be.

Two weeks into the new town, three weeks into the new school, the problem had acquired numbers. Ms. Hughes, who taught his English elective, had mentioned offhand one afternoon that a 2018 study by a communication researcher named Jeffrey Hall estimated it took roughly fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Mason had written it in the margin of his notebook without knowing why, and then found himself doing arithmetic during lunch. Forty minutes a day, if someone actually sat with him, and nobody reliably did. Two weeks in, he had maybe eleven hours total, and that was counting the boy in his physics class who had lent him a calculator and explained the seating chart. Eleven hours, and fifty required, and senior year was one year long. It nearly worked out, if he did the math generously, and he had done the math generously, twice.

He told none of this to Kaiya, because telling it would have codified it, turned a floaty dread into a document with figures, and documents like that demanded responses. He told Mackenzie instead, late at night, over a call that kept dropping in the hills.

"Fifty hours," Mackenzie said. "Is that for a best friend?"

"Casual friend. Casual. A best friend is probably, like, a thousand."

"We have a thousand. Easily. I've known you since we were nine."

"That's what I mean," Mason said. "We already have it banked. You two don't need me there for it to stay true."

There was a silence on the line that had static in it but wasn't only static. "That's a very you way of saying you're lonely," Mackenzie said.

In the car, now, with the trailer thumping and the new town eleven hours behind them because it was Thanksgiving and his father had decided they were driving back for it, Mason finally typed. He wrote: I did the math. There's this study from 2018, a researcher named Jeffrey Hall, he estimated about fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. I'm at maybe eleven with the whole town. But there's a guy in physics, Dev doesn't count, his name is Dev, and a girl named Priya who argued with me about existentialism until the bus came, and I'm going to get to fifty with them or I'm not, and either way I'll know why. I'm not saying it's the same. I'm saying it's not nothing. He looked at it, decided it was too long, and sent it anyway.

His father took the exit toward home, toward the old street, and the streetlights came on all at once the way they did in November. "You want to drive the last mile?" his father asked. "You've got your license."

"Traffic's bad."

"It's not."

Mason took the wheel at the gas station by the church, and the car felt different from the driver's seat, smaller and more his. He drove past the school, dark except for the gym, past the corner where Mackenzie had crashed her bike in eighth grade, and parked in front of Kaiya's house because his father said nothing when he signaled the turn. She was on the porch before he fully stopped, jacket over pajamas, and she opened the passenger door and leaned across the console to look at him.

"Fifty hours," she said. "You loser. You made a spreadsheet out of missing us."

Mason said, "It's in a notebook."

"Same thing." She stayed there, half in the car, one foot still on the curb, and behind her the porch light buzzed and flickered. "Get out. Ten minutes. I'll bank you the first hour right now."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which did not reveal that its author was a woman.
story:
Cameron had promised himself he would leave the library by nine, and the clock above the returns desk was already at 8:41, its second hand ticking with what felt like personal malice. The essay was due first period. Mr. Mehta had been blunt about it: apply a feminist or a Marxist lens to a passage from Jane Eyre, a real passage, quoted and argued, not waved at. Cameron had chosen the passage days ago, the one where Jane stands on the rooftop at Thornfield and longs for a "power of vision" beyond the horizon, for a world of women and men alike. He had underlined it so many times the paper had gone soft.

The problem was the lens. He had spent the week titrating between the two readings, adding a little of one, testing, adding the other, and the mixture kept refusing to settle. The feminist reading made the rooftop passage sing: Jane's hunger wasn't romantic, it was economic, a governess with almost nothing claiming a right to want. The Marxist reading made the same passage into a cleaner indictment: whatever Jane wanted, the machinery of inheritance and employment had already priced it. Both were true. Neither was complete. He had eleven sentences on his laptop and all of them began with "Perhaps."

Sahil arrived at 8:50 with a paper bag of chips and no apology. He dropped into the chair across from Cameron and peeled the bag open with a sound like a small landslide. "You're still on paragraph one," he said. "I can see it from here."

"I'm on paragraph three," Cameron said. "Paragraphs one and two are just unwritten."

Zara came a minute later, hair still damp from swim practice, and set down a photocopy she'd made of a title page. She slid it across the table. "This is why I texted you. My grandmother's cleaning out my grandfather's study. Look at what she found."

The page was a reproduction of an old edition, the paper browned at the edges. Cameron bent over it. Under the title, Jane Eyre, the name of the author was printed plainly: Currer Bell. He read it twice. "Who's Currer Bell?"

"That's the thing," Zara said. "Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which didn't reveal that its author was a woman."

Sahil stopped chewing. "So the book everyone calls a woman's classic came out under a man's name?"

"Under a name that didn't say either way," Zara said. "Currer isn't obviously anything. That's the point."

Cameron sat back. Something in the essay reorganized itself without his permission. The rooftop passage, the governess longing for a wider life, had been written by someone who had to hide her own name to be read at all. The two lenses he'd been trying to keep in separate beakers weren't separate. If a woman's authorship had to be concealed to reach the market, then the gendered constraint and the market were one system, not two. He typed fast, not caring that his first sentences were clumsy, because the shape was finally there.

Mr. Mehta passed their table on his way to lock the study room, keys jingling, and paused when he saw the photocopy. He looked at it, then at Cameron's screen, and said nothing for a moment. "You found the Bell page," he said at last. "Half my students never notice the pseudonym. They read the title and skip everything under it."

"It's not a pseudonym exactly," Cameron said. "It's a shield. Or a costume." He wasn't sure which, and said so.

"That uncertainty," Mr. Mehta said, "is the essay. Write that." He tapped the table twice and moved on toward the front desk.

Sahil had drifted to the shelves and come back with a book of Victorian history, which he now held open like evidence in a trial. "There's chicanery everywhere in this," he said. "Fake names, fake reviews, critics pretending the novel's morality shocked them when what shocked them was who might have written it."

"Or they genuinely didn't know," Zara said. "That's worse, kind of. The whole reading public arguing about a book, and the person who made it can't raise her hand."

Cameron wrote that down. The library announcement came over the speakers, ten minutes to closing, and the lights in the far stacks dimmed as if in sympathy. He worked through the announcement, through the shuffling of bags around him, through Sahil eating the last of the chips in careful, rationed bites beside him. The paragraph he was building said this: the Marxist lens explained the rooftop as hunger shaped by class, the feminist lens explained it as hunger shaped by gender, and the Currer Bell title page showed why he refused to pick. A writer hidden from the market was hidden in both directions at once. But the paragraph also said, and he let it say, that he couldn't prove Brontë's reasons from a name on a copied page. The pseudonym was a fact. The motive behind it was a guess. He kept the fact and marked the guess as a guess.

At 9:12 Zara pulled the chair out from under his foot, gently, and he saved the file. Eight hundred words, some of it good, one paragraph he'd rewrite on the bus. The gain and the loss sat together in his chest: he had a position at last, and the position had a hole in it he could see clear through. Sahil held the door. Outside, the streetlights were on, and Zara was folding the photocopy to keep it, the name Currer Bell disappearing into the crease.

"Tomorrow," Sahil said, "you tell me if Mehta buys it."

"If he doesn't," Cameron said, zipping his bag, "at least I bought it."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: 'Ibid.' abbreviates the Latin 'ibidem', meaning 'in the same place', and is used in a note citing the same source as the note just before it.
story:
Kyle found the word on page four of the article Mr. Ong had photocopied for the whole class, and he read the line three times before he decided the copier had made a mistake. The footnotes ran down the page like a list of debts. Note fourteen said something about a German historian and gave a title. Note fifteen said only "Ibid." and then a page number. Note sixteen said "Ibid." again.

He raised his hand. "What's Ibid?"

Mr. Ong, who was reticent at the best of times and never answered a question he thought a student could answer herself, turned to the class. "Does anyone want that one?"

Jenna, who sat near the window with her bibliography already drafted, looked up from her notebook. "My mom writes history. She says it all over her drafts. It's Latin. Ibidem. It means 'in the same place.'"

"In the same place," Kyle repeated.

"It's used in a note citing the same source as the note just before it," Jenna said. "So fifteen is the same book as fourteen. Sixteen too."

Kyle wrote this in the margin of his photocopy, then wrote it again on his hand, because margins washed off in his backpack. It was the first thing all semester that had made the footnotes feel like a system instead of a curse.

The paper was due in nine days, and Kyle had a problem bigger than any single word. He wanted to argue that the city had torn down the Easton Street viaduct in 1961 because of money, not because of the engineering report, which is what everyone said at the time. But the sources disagreed. The newspaper archive said insolvency, the comptroller's report said the bridge was sound, and a retired engineer quoted in an oral history said both things in the same interview. Kyle had two ways of thinking and no way to hold them at once. His father, who fixed furnaces for a living, had told him that when two gauges disagreed you trusted neither one and went to look at the pipe. But Kyle could not go look at a decision made twenty years before he was born.

He stayed after class on Thursday, not to ask Mr. Ong what to think, because he knew better, but to ask about the citation style. "If I cite the comptroller's report three times in a row," he said, "do I have to write the whole thing out each time?"

"What do you think, given what you learned Tuesday?"

Kyle thought. "Ibid?"

Mr. Ong almost smiled. "Typeset it in italics. And Kyle, the page numbers still matter. Same place doesn't mean same page."

That was the detail that unglued something in him. The report could say the bridge was sound on page twelve and say the repair budget had coagulated into a deficit on page ninety, and both quotes could be true, and he could cite the same source twice without pretending it spoke with one voice. The disagreement he had been treating as an obstacle was the evidence. He went home and wrote four pages that night, footnotes marching down the bottom of each one, "Ibid., 91." and "Ibid., 12." like a conversation the document was having with itself.

Jenna had her own want, which she had mentioned only once, in October, and Kyle had remembered it because she had said it quietly. She wanted the Ong scholarship, and the research paper was a third of the grade it was decided on. Friday she came to the library table where Kyle was checking his bibliography against the style sheet, and she stood there with her draft held against her chest.

"Can you look at mine?" she said. "Just the citations. You understand them better than I do now, which is annoying."

He read her footnotes. Her fourth note and fifth note cited the same book, but she had written the full title twice, and her eighth cited a different source and should not have been Ibid. at all. He marked both places with a pencil and slid it back. "Same source twice in a row, you can shorten it. But check the one before. If it's a different book, you have to write it out."

She found the error herself, which he could tell was what she'd wanted, the way she sat back and tapped the page. "Okay," she said. "Okay, that's fixable."

On the day the papers came back, Mr. Ong set Kyle's on the desk with the grade face down, which was his custom, so that you could choose when to know. Kyle turned his over. At the top, in red, Mr. Ong had written a single sentence: The evidence contradicts itself and so do you, on page six and page eight. This is a strength, but say so. Kyle read it twice. He had not solved the viaduct question, and he suspected now that no one would, that the money and the engineering had been tangled together in a room he could never enter. He closed the paper and looked across the room at Jenna, who was still holding hers against her chest, unread.

"Turn it over," he said.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: A 2010 study claimed 'power poses' raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, but a larger 2015 replication found no such hormonal effect, though people still reported feeling more powerful.
story:
Mr. Toussaint had turned the back half of the library into an interview room, one folding table, two chairs, and a paper sign that read PART-TIME HIRE PRACTICE. Sebastian sat in the hallway outside with his application folded into quarters inside a folder he'd borrowed from his mother. He had an actual interview on Saturday, at the garden centre on Marsh Road, and Mr. Toussaint had agreed to run him through the thing twice before then.

Brogan came out of the interview room looking morose, his shoulders dropped like wet cardboard. "He asked why I left my last job and I said my manager was, quote, a piece of work. He wrote something down. He actually wrote something down."

"That's fine. They always write something down." Imogen was next in line, though she seemed in no hurry, leaning against the wall with her sneakers crossed at the ankle. She looked at Sebastian's hands. "You've refolded that application four times."

"Twice." He smoothed it flat on his knees anyway. "I keep looking at the floor when I answer things. Saturday, the guy's going to think I'm hiding something."

Brogan brightened a little, glad for a problem that wasn't his. "You should do the pose thing. Imogen's cousin did it before her interview at the bank." He stood up straight, planted his feet wide, and put his fists on his hips like a man about to fight a weather system. "Power pose. Two minutes in the bathroom. It raises your testosterone."

Sebastian considered him. "Where'd you hear that?"

"Some video. It was a study or something."

Imogen pushed off the wall. "That part's shaky, actually. My psych teacher had us look it up. There was a study in 2010 that said power poses raised testosterone and lowered cortisol, but then a bigger one in 2015 tried it again and found no hormonal effect at all." She shrugged. "The people still said they felt more powerful, though. So it does something. Just not the chemicals."

"So it's fake," Brogan said, letting his arms drop.

"So it's not fake fake," Imogen said. "It's fake where it counts for hormones and real where it counts for feelings. Anyway. I'm up." She went in, and Sebastian heard Mr. Toussaint's low, pleasant voice start in on her.

He sat with it. He had been planning to be honest about everything on Saturday, and here was a thing that was honest in a split way: standing like a superhero wouldn't change his blood, but it might change his morning. His father would say that was cheating yourself. His sister would say nobody cares about the mechanism if the porch light works. He asked the hallway water fountain, which had no opinion, and then it was his turn.

Mr. Toussaint shook his hand across the folding table. "So, Sebastian. Tell me why you want to work at Hollis Garden Centre."

Sebastian answered, and watched his own gaze slide down to the folder, to the table edge, to a scuff on the linoleum. Mr. Toussaint let the silence stretch. "Look at me when you say it," he said, not unkindly. "Not the whole time. Just enough that I believe you."

"It's not that I don't believe it. It's that looking at people feels like claiming something."

"Claim it, then." Mr. Toussaint made a note. "Again."

They ran it twice more, and on the third try Sebastian kept his eyes up through a whole answer about carrying flats of marigolds one summer for a neighbour who'd broken her wrist, how he'd gone back the next week unasked, less to expiate his guilt for not offering sooner than because the watering was genuinely satisfying, the smell of wet soil in the morning. The second interview had been better than the first, and Sebastian had made a kind of reparation to himself for the first one simply by doing it again. That felt like a truer sentence than any pose could produce, though he couldn't have explained the difference out loud.

Saturday morning, he was early, so he used the garden centre's customer restroom. He caught his own eye in the mirror, remembered Brogan standing in the hallway with his fists on his hips, remembered Imogen saying no hormonal effect at all, and stood there anyway, feet wide, chin level, for close to two minutes. He didn't feel like a different person. He felt like a person who had decided to stay in the room with his own reflection, which turned out to be most of the battle.

The manager, a broad woman with dirt permanently under her thumbnail, asked him the first question, and Sebastian looked at her and said, "Because I'm good with things that need steady attention, and I can prove it."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Japan's Buddhist festival of Obon, families light fires to welcome the spirits of ancestors home, and at the end many float lanterns down rivers to guide the spirits back.
story:
The morning after Angelina arrived in Sakata, her aunt handed her a bundle of incense sticks and a paper bag and said they were going to the cemetery before it got hot. This was the third day of Obon, her aunt explained on the walk, the days when the spirits of ancestors come home, and the family had lit a small fire at the gate the night before to welcome her grandfather back. Angelina had been in Japan for two weeks of language classes and awkward dinners, and no one had told her that the grandfather she had met exactly four times was going to be part of the itinerary.

The cemetery sat on a hill above the rice fields, rows of grey stone markers with carved names and family crests, each one fronted by a shallow basin and a shelf for flowers. Her grandfather's stone had the family name on it and a tall thin stalk of dried grass someone had left, which her aunt replaced with fresh chrysanthemums from the paper bag. Then the aunt lit the incense, set it upright in the gravel, and pressed her palms together. Angelina stood beside her with her own incense burning and did not know what to do with her hands.

Back at the house, she found the messages she had been avoiding. Elyse had written, "You don't have to do anything. You didn't really know him, so it's fine to just let it be weird for a week." Zaynab had written, "When my nana died I made myself go to everything, even the hospital, and I'm glad. Skip it and you'll regret it, I think." Both of them meant well. Both of them were talking about a situation that was not quite hers, because her grandfather had died in April and her mother had said not to come, that missing the term would be an indictment of how little Angelina had prioritized school all year, and Angelina had obeyed and had felt wrong about it every day since.

Her mother, when Angelina called her that evening, was blunt as always. "He was difficult. He was irascible his whole life and he didn't soften for anyone, including me. I went back for the funeral. That's what I owed him. You lighting a candle isn't going to fix anything." Her mother's way was to settle accounts, close them, move on. Her aunt's way, as far as Angelina could tell, was the opposite: the account never closed, because the grandfather was still arriving, every August, down the smoke of a small fire at the gate.

On the last evening of Obon, the whole family walked to the river. Her cousin carried a stack of paper lanterns, and the aunt knelt on the bank with a marker and wrote the family name on the side of one, then a smaller character underneath. "What's the small one?" Angelina asked. "His name," the cousin said. "The lantern carries him back. This is how we send the spirits home at the end." The cousin said it the way someone tells you which bus goes downtown, without ceremony, and Angelina found that more convincing than any speech would have been.

There were dozens of people on the bank already, and a man in rubber boots standing in the shallows, catching each lantern as it was released and steadying it into the current so it would not snag. Angelina's aunt lit the candle inside their lantern with a long match, cupping the flame against the breeze. She looked up at Angelina and offered the lantern, and Angelina took it in both hands. It was lighter than she expected, just paper and a wire frame and a small wobbling light, and it was carrying an irascible old man she had met four times, who had once told her at a dinner that her Japanese was terrible, which it was.

She did not know whether she believed the lantern was actually going anywhere, or whether her grandfather was anywhere to go from. Zayb's version, where ritual was a debt you paid so you would not regret it, did not feel right either, sitting there with the paper warm against her palms. What she thought, kneeling at the water's edge, was that both her mother and her aunt were doing something true: one closed a door, and the other kept a light on inside it, and maybe a person could do both, could say this is finished and also come back every August with flowers and a fire and a lantern. She could not have defended that in an essay. She filed it under things she would understand later, or never.

"Both hands," the cousin said, "or the wind takes it sideways."

Angelina leaned forward and set the lantern on the water, holding it until the current tugged it away from her fingers, and watched it join the slow procession of lights moving down the dark river toward the sea.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety guidance says perishable food should not sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours, or one hour when it is above 90 degrees.
story:
The chicken had sat out from two in the afternoon until almost seven, and David kept doing the arithmetic on the bus to school, subtracting and re-subtracting as though the hours might come out differently the fourth time. Five hours. He could still smell the cookout on his jacket, charcoal and his uncle's cigar, and beneath that the sweetish sourness of the aluminum tray his mother had carried into the kitchen at midnight, foil crimped tight, everything saved, nothing thrown away.

In Mr. Marino's cooking classroom the ovens were already ticking through their preheat, and the overhead vents made their low cathedral hum. Mr. Marino had assigned them each to plan a full family meal, cooked and carried home by Friday, and David had chosen the cookout as his theme, a reimagined version of Saturday, done right. He was dicing an onion at the steel counter when Desirae slid in across from him and set down a container of potato salad.

"Guess what my grandmother made me bring," she said, popping the lid. "She thinks you're too skinny."

Trinity leaned over from the pasta station, wooden spoon in hand like a gavel. "Wait. Is that from your cookout? The one on Saturday?"

"My family's cookout, yeah." He heard himself say it before he thought. "We left everything out on the table all afternoon. Then we ate again at night."

Trinity winced, actually winced, the way people do at a bad grade. "Perishable food isn't supposed to sit between 40 and 140 degrees for more than two hours. One hour if it's above 90 outside." She said it flat and fast, like something she'd memorized off the wall of her mother's restaurant kitchen, where she'd worked summers since she was fourteen. "It was like 95 on Saturday."

David stood with the knife still in the onion. Two hours. He replayed the afternoon: the trays going out at two, his uncles playing horseshoes, nobody covering anything, the mayonnaise-based salad sweating in the sun, the chicken turning slowly in its own heat. Five hours, at ninety-five degrees, which meant the safe window had closed an hour after the food hit the table.

"So everything's bad," he said. "The chicken, the salad, all of it."

"Anything perishable that sat out, yeah." Trinity went back to her pasta, but she glanced at him sideways. "Was it covered at least?"

"Does covering matter?" he asked, and realized as he asked it that this was the kind of question he liked, the kind where you had to separate what felt true from what was. He'd spent a whole semester half-listening in philosophy club while Desirae argued about epistemology, how you know the things you think you know, and here it was again in a foil tray: his mother believed the leftovers were fine because they looked fine, smelled fine, and belief had been standing in for evidence since the invention of refrigerators.

Desirae poked her potato salad with a fork. "My grandmother would say the smoke kept the flies off, so it's fine."

"The smoke kept the flies off," Trinity agreed. "That part's true. It's just not the part that matters."

The bell hadn't rung yet and the ovens were climbing toward temperature, the kitchen filling with the dry smell of heating steel. David pulled out his phone under the counter and texted his mother, typing and deleting twice before he kept it simple: don't eat the leftovers from Saturday, I'll explain tonight, I'm making dinner instead. Then he looked up at the two of them, this small strange relief moving through him that had nothing to do with being right.

He thought of how the tray had looked last night under the kitchen light, the chicken glistening faintly, innocent, almost malevolent in its calm, and how nothing about it had announced itself as dangerous. That was the part that would keep him curious for weeks. No smell, no color, no warning. Just a number you had to know beforehand.

Mr. Marino wandered past with his clipboard. "David, your mise en place is looking a little philosophical." He tapped the cutting board. "Onion, then peppers."

"Onion, then peppers," David said, and lowered the blade, and the first clean cut released its sharpness into the air.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources.
story:
The radiator under the window ticked like a slow clock, and the maps on the wall had faded to the color of weak tea. Cole sat with the project brief flat in front of him: model how Fernvale's growth over fifty years would strain its reservoir. He was supposed to be choosing a partner. Shaelyn had already moved her chair toward Harlow's desk before the bell finished ringing.

"You're with me," Mr. Byrne said, dropping a printed article on Cole's desk. "Since you don't seem to be in a hurry." He walked off before Cole could answer. The article was a scan of something old, the type small and smudged, and the title read The Limits to Growth. Cole turned it over. On the back, in Byrne's handwriting: Start here. Don't stop here.

At lunch he read it in the stairwell where the vending machine hummed and the air smelled of burnt coffee. The book had been published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, and they had used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources. That was the line he copied into his notebook, twice, because the first time his hand had skipped the "3." He liked the shape of the idea: five things tied together, so that pulling one pulled the rest.

"It's called World3," he said to Shaelyn in class the next day, showing her the notebook. She was filling in a spreadsheet on Harlow's laptop, columns of housing starts and pump capacity for Fernvale.

"Cool name," she said, not looking up.

"No, listen. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources. They linked them. That's what we should do with the reservoir. Not just houses equals water. Houses plus jobs plus farm runoff plus the tax base that pays for the treatment plant."

Harlow leaned back in his chair. "Byrne wants a table and a graph. My brother did this project two years ago. You draw the lake, you draw the houses, you get an A."

"Your brother drew a lake."

Harlow shrugged, which was its own kind of argument. Shaelyn, though, had stopped typing. She turned the laptop so Cole could see the spreadsheet, and her columns were already more tangled than Harlow knew: school enrollment, which depended on young families, who came for the manufacturing plant, whose effluent fed the creek that fed the reservoir. "I kept adding things," she said. "It wouldn't stay simple."

That was the moment. Cole dragged his chair over, and for three days the three of them built it in the geography room after last bell, with the janitor's radio going faintly down the hall and the radiator ticking on. They made index cards for each variable and taped them to the whiteboard with yarn between them, operationalizing the vague stuff into numbers they could actually get: remuneration at the plant translated into household water use, since the town's own billing data showed usage rising with income. It was Harlow who found the wastewater reports in the town office basement, coming upstairs with dust on his sleeves and the papers held out like something he'd caught. "It's congenital with this town," he said, half joking. "Every boom, they run the water short. 1958. 1979. 2002."

The twist came on presentation day. Cole stood at the front with the yarn diagram behind him and explained the linkages, and Mr. Byrne listened with his arms folded, saying nothing, which Cole had learned to read as either approval or ambush. When Cole said the model would show Fernvale hitting a water ceiling around year forty, Byrne asked one question: "What did World3 actually predict, and what happened?"

Cole's mouth went dry. He had the fact but not the aftermath; he had stopped where the handwriting told him to stop. The room was quiet except for the radiator. The smell of chalk dust and the radiator's hot metal filled his head.

"I don't know," Cole said. "That's honest. I know what it linked. I don't know yet if it was right." He looked at Shaelyn, then at the yarn web on the board. "People argue about it. We'd have to read the arguments, not just the summary."

Byrne uncrossed his arms. "Then your graph is a question, not an answer."

"Yes," Cole said. "But it's a better question than the lake drawing."

Byrne wrote something in his binder, face unreadable, and called the next group. Shaelyn squeezed Cole's shoulder as they walked back. Harlow was already folding the yarn off the whiteboard, looping it around his hand. "Keep the cards," he said. "I want to see what happens when we take the plant away and put a bottling company in instead."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The video showed a flooded street where the water seemed to undulate like something alive, boats nosing past shopfronts, a man on a roof waving a red shirt. Below it, in the thread, people were furious. Their town, someone said. Last night, someone else said. Anna had watched it three times already, her finger hovering over the share button, when Jules leaned across the aisle of the computer lab and whispered, "Just post it. Everyone's posting it."

The lab was half empty, third period study hall, the monitors casting pale light on the rows of empty desks behind them. Ms. Addo sat at the front marking papers, and somewhere a printer ground through a worksheet nobody would collect. Anna had come in intending to finish her chemistry write-up. Instead she had opened her phone under the desk, seen the video, and felt the familiar pull, the one that made sharing feel like helping.

"Wait," she said. "Hold on." She said it mostly to herself.

She thought of her mother, last spring, standing at the kitchen counter with her own phone held out like evidence. A grainy clip of a politician saying something monstrous, forwarded from a cousin, forwarded from who knows where. Her mother had been ready to be outraged for a week. Anna, scrolling later that night out of boredom, had found the same clip on a fact-checking site with a date from two years before and different subtitles. She had shown her mother, and her mother had gone quiet, then defensive, then finally said, "Well, somebody said it sometime," which was somehow worse than if she'd just been wrong.

Here in the lab, Anna opened a search engine and dragged the video's thumbnail into the image search bar. Jules watched over her shoulder, chewing the end of a pen. The results loaded slowly, the little progress bar crawling while the radiator ticked.

The video was real. That was the strange part. It was genuine footage of a real flood. But the results put it four years earlier and on a different continent, from a news agency whose name Anna recognized, with the original report attached. Someone had lifted it, stripped the caption, and set it loose in a new context where it looked like proof of something that hadn't happened.

"See, it's real," Jules said. "So what's the problem?"

"The flood's real. The claim isn't. It says last night. It says it's here." Anna pointed at the date stamp burned into the reposted version, which the original didn't have. "Somebody added that."

Nelson, two rows up, turned around. He was the kind of person who read the terms of service for fun, and he'd once spent an entire lunch period explaining junk mail filters to anyone who would listen. "You're doing the SIFT thing," he said. "My cousin taught me. Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their original context. That's what the S in it stands for, stopping before you share."

"I didn't know it had a name," Anna said.

"Mike Caulfield. Some educator guy. It's a whole method." Nelson shrugged, as if to say the name had cost him nothing to know.

Ms. Addo looked up from her marking. "Quiet, please," she said, but without any force behind it, and went back to her red pen.

Anna ran the rest of it in her head. Stop: she had, barely, the share button still untouched. Investigate the source: the account that reposted it had no history, no location, a username of random consonants. Find better coverage: the news agency's original report was right there, with the date, the place, the names of the streets. Trace the claim: done, the thumbnail search had led her straight back to it. It had taken her maybe four minutes.

She typed a reply in the thread, then deleted it. What was the point of arguing with strangers? Then she thought of her mother's face at the kitchen counter, the clip held out like a gift, and she typed it again, shorter this time: original footage is from 2021, different country, here's the link. She posted it. Her hands felt stupidly shaky, as if she'd done something gratuitous, something showy, when really she'd done the minimum. Maybe nobody would read it. Maybe the next person to see the video would share it anyway, and the next, the outrage undulating through the feeds the way the water had moved through that street, finding every low place.

Jules was quiet for a moment, pen still between her teeth. Then she said, "Okay. Send me the original, then. The real one. If people are going to be upset about a flood, it might as well be the right flood."

Anna found the agency's report and forwarded it. On the front page of the thread, the video was still gathering shares, the counter climbing in its indifferent way. She refreshed once, twice. Then her reply appeared at the top, one line in a rising tide, and someone beneath it had written, "Checked. She's right."

"So," Jules said, "what do we do about the cousin who keeps sending my mom this stuff?"

Anna pulled out a notebook and wrote, in the margin of her chemistry notes, four letters. "We start there."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In plant and animal cells, introns are cut out of newly made RNA and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
story:
The trail behind the school cut through a strip of woods too narrow to get lost in, which was exactly why Robert liked it. He walked it with his biology notebook open in one hand, mouthing the words he was supposed to have learned two weeks ago. Transcription. Translation. The vocabulary swam. On Monday he had a retake, and Ms. Chea had told him, without cruelty, that a C-minus was not a grade so much as a symptom.

Desiree was already at the bend by the creek, sitting on a flat rock with her phone propped against her water bottle, filming herself. She was making a video for the environmental club, six takes in and getting belligerent about the wind moving her hair. "Every single one has a plane going over," she said when she saw him. "Or a dog. Or me saying 'um.' It's unusable."

Robert sat down on the other end of the rock and watched her scroll through the footage, dragging clips around with her thumb, cutting out the ruined takes and pushing the good ones together so they ran as one. She deleted a stretch where she'd stumbled over the word "watershed," then another where a jogger had passed behind her, then snapped the two clean halves of the sentence back to back until the video flowed. It took her about four minutes.

He looked at his notebook. In his notes, copied off the board, there was a diagram of a gene with thick segments and thin ones, labeled exons and introns, and an arrow showing something happening to the RNA before it left the nucleus. He had never actually understood what happened there. He had just drawn the arrow and hoped.

"Wait," he said. "Do that again. The cutting part."

Desiree gave him a look but humored him, splitting a clip, deleting the middle, joining the ends. "Like that. The bad part's gone and the sentence still works."

"In plant and animal cells," Robert said slowly, reading his own handwriting as if it might betray him, "introns are cut out of newly made RNA, and the remaining exons are spliced together before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus." He looked up. "Spliced. That's your word. That's literally what you just did. You cut out the bad takes and spliced the good ones."

"You're comparing my video to your cells right now."

"I'm comparing my cells to your video. You're the nucleus." He was half laughing, but underneath it something had clicked open, the way a lock does when you stop forcing it. The gene was the raw footage, all of it, every stuttering take. The finished messenger RNA was her final cut. And the cell did the editing before anything shipped out.

He tried to explain it to Holden that afternoon, when Holden joined them on the trail with two energy drinks and no notebook. Holden was the kind of student who wanted to litigate every test question afterward, who would corner Ms. Chea after class and argue that the wording of number four had been ambiguous, and who had scored better than Robert on the first attempt without, as far as Robert could tell, understanding any of it. Robert gave him the video analogy, and Holden shrugged and said, "So it's just cutting stuff out. Fine. I'll memorize it."

"It's not memorizing," Robert said, and then found he couldn't say what it was instead. He could feel the shape of an idea without being able to finish it: that Holden's way and his way were both real, that some things could be memorized and some had to be built, and that he had spent three years doing only the first and calling it studying. Last spring he had dropped out of the debate team a week before regionals because the work felt endless, and he had told himself it was discipline, a kind of asceticism, giving up one thing to protect his grades. Sitting on the rock now, he suspected it had just been quitting with better manners. He didn't say any of this out loud.

Instead he asked Desiree if he could watch her edit again, and she said fine but she was narrating her own project, so he'd have to be quiet. He watched her finger split the clip, remove the dead middle, and press the two living ends together. Before it leaves the nucleus, he thought. Before it goes anywhere, it gets cut down to what matters.

He walked home the long way, along the creek, reciting the whole thing under his breath: the gene is copied, the introns are cut out, the exons are spliced, the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus and then, somewhere beyond the diagram, gets read off into protein. He understood the splicing now because he had watched a girl do it with her thumb. Whether that would survive until Monday, whether the retake would reward understanding or only reward it accidentally, he couldn't know. Ms. Chea might ask it straight and he might blank anyway. That part stayed open.

On Monday morning he found the question, number seven, worth six points, and there was a blank diagram with an arrow pointing at the space between the gene and the messenger RNA. Robert wrote: introns cut out, exons spliced together, before it leaves the nucleus. Then, underneath, he drew a small phone and wrote "like editing video" in the margin, and crossed it out, and left the cross-out visible, because he wanted to see later which half of him had gotten it right.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: A Danish study published in 2019 followed more than 650,000 children and found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism, even among children with autistic siblings.
story:
Jackson had eleven tabs open, which was nine more than the essay required, and the clock in the corner of the screen said 11:14. The assignment, due at midnight in Mr. Fernando's dropbox, had seemed easy on Monday: take a scientific claim, find two studies that disagree, and write about which one you would trust. He had planned to knock it out in an hour. Instead he had spent the week at Jaden's kitchen table arguing about it, and now he was down to forty-six minutes with nothing on the page but his name.

The claim was the MMR vaccine and autism, because Jaden's mother believed it, and Jaden had inherited the belief the way you inherit a coat, without ever checking whether it fit. Jaden had sent him a study that morning, triumphant, a screenshot of twelve children whose parents said symptoms began after the shot. Twelve kids, Jackson kept thinking. His stats teacher had once said something about sample size that he'd ignored in favor of the window, and now he wanted it back.

He typed "MMR autism large study" into the search bar and scrolled past the first page, which was mostly people shouting. On the second page he found a Danish study from 2019, and the number stopped him: more than 650,000 children. He read the line twice. It followed all of them and found no link between the vaccine and autism, even among children who had autistic siblings, which was the part that seemed to close every escape route. If autism ran in your family and you still didn't develop it after the shot, the family-history argument had nowhere left to stand.

He opened a chat window. "found something," he wrote to Jaden. "danish study. 650000 kids. no link, even with autistic siblings." The typing indicator pulsed for a long time. "theres a study with 12 kids that says the opposite," Jaden finally wrote, and Jackson could hear the shrug in it. He looked at the two numbers side by side on his screen, twelve and 650,000, and understood for the first time that they were not the same kind of thing at all. One was an anecdote wearing a lab coat. The other was a population.

Then he noticed something else, which was the part that would actually go in the essay. The Danish paper was not alone. Other teams had run other children, in other countries, and the result kept coming out the same way; journals had other researchers read it before publishing and picked at it, and still it held. Nobody had declared it true from a podium. It had been true over and over, on different days, in different places, by people who had reasons to wish it were false. The twelve-child paper, when he dug into its history, turned out to have been withdrawn years ago, its conclusions disowned by most of its own authors, though the screenshot Jaden's mother kept on her phone did not mention that part.

It occurred to him that he could impugn the twelve-child researchers' honesty, call them frauds and be done, but the essay didn't need that and neither did Jaden. A small study was not a lie. It was just a small study, a friable thing that crumbled when you leaned the weight of everyone else's work against it. That felt like the counterpoint worth writing: not that one side was evil, but that one claim had survived being checked and one had not. He started typing, fast, the keys clattering in the quiet house, and at 11:52 he pasted in the paragraph about the Danish children and their siblings and hit submit at 11:58.

His phone buzzed before the confirmation email did. Jaden again: "ok but my mom says scientists change their minds all the time." Jackson sat back and looked at that, because it was true and also exactly backwards. The consensus he had just written about was nothing but scientists changing their minds, slowly, in public, each one trying to be the person who found the flaw. Changing their minds was the method. He typed "yeah" and then deleted it, and then typed: "come by tomorrow, i'll show you what i found. bring your mom's study."

There was no reply for a minute, and then: "she doesn't have the study. she has a screenshot of an article about the study." Jackson laughed once, alone in the kitchen dark, and closed his eleven tabs.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation.
story:
The message arrived at 9:47 on a Tuesday night, while Mason was folding towels he had no intention of putting away. Marius had sent a photo of the grocery store on Delmore Street, taken through the window from the bus stop, and beneath it a single line: they're putting in the machines.

Mason looked at the photo for a long moment. Four self-checkout kiosks stood in a row where the express lanes used to be, still wrapped in plastic like patients waiting for surgery. He typed "which machines" and then deleted it, because the answer was obvious, and because he already knew what the answer meant for him. He had been a cashier there since June. Two shifts a week, sometimes three, scanning cereal and asking whether people wanted their milk in a bag.

Maren responded before he could decide what else to say. "My dad's store did that last spring. They kept two people on." Marius sent a shrugging emoji, then, "corporate loves it. fewer of us to pay." Mason put the phone face down on his bed and picked up the towel again, but the chat kept pinging, and he kept hearing, underneath the pings, the beep of his own register, a sound he had come to find almost soothing, like a metronome for other people's groceries.

He typed slowly, because the thought was still forming. "it's not just us though. there's this study." He had read about it months ago, in a magazine in the dentist's waiting room, and had copied the number into his phone because numbers felt like things worth keeping. He found the note. "a 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation." He sent it, then added, "not just cashiers."

Maren's reply came fast. "47 percent? that's basically half the country." Marius, slower: "half of everybody I know works those jobs. my brother drives a truck." There was a pause in the conversation then, the kind of pause that happens even in a group chat, three dots appearing and disappearing, someone starting a sentence and abandoning it.

Mason sat on the floor with his back against the bed. He thought about Ms. Fernando, his history teacher, who had spent a week in the spring on enclosure laws, on how land that people had used for generations was fenced off and turned to someone else's profit. She had used the word expropriate, taking something away from the people who held it, and at the time it had seemed like a museum word, belonging to grainy photographs and long-dead farmers. He typed it now, hesitated, and instead wrote what he actually meant. "the machines don't take the money exactly. they take the shift. same thing though?"

He regretted the question mark as soon as he sent it. It made him sound unsure, and he was unsure, but not in the soft way the punctuation implied. He was unsure in the way that mattered, holding two ideas at once and not being able to make them lie flat against each other. Because the machines were also, he had to admit, not nothing. The lines at his register on Sunday afternoons went back past the magazines. Old people struggled with the chip readers and hated being rushed. If the kiosks shortened those lines, was that theft or was that progress, and who got to decide which word applied?

Maren, who wanted to study statistics, was already pulling at the thread. "it says at high risk. not that they'll all disappear." Marius pushed back. "tell that to my paycheck." Mason watched them go back and forth, two friends arguing in short blue bubbles, and found that he agreed with both of them, which was an uncomfortable place to stand. He thought about his manager, Mr. Okafor, who had hired him and had said, on his first day, that the store was like a small town. Mason had liked that idea, a small town with registers. He liked it less now that the town seemed to be governed by people none of them had ever met, a distant board whose decisions arrived as plastic-wrapped machines and memos about redeployment. Oligarchy, he thought, was probably too strong a word for a grocery store, but the shape of the feeling was the same.

The next afternoon he walked to Delmore Street before his shift. A technician in gray coveralls was calibrating one of the kiosks, tapping a screen, and the putative customers of the future, as far as Mason could tell, were the technician himself and a boy of about ten who kept scanning his own hand for fun. Mr. Okafor stood nearby with a clipboard. He looked tired but not grim, and when he saw Mason he waved him over and said the store would need someone to supervise the kiosks, to clear jams and check IDs for beer, and that corporate called the position "front-end attendant." Mason said, "so same job, different register." Mr. Okafor shrugged one shoulder, the way he did when a memo had said something he hadn't decided yet whether to believe.

That night the chat lit up again. Marius had heard from his cousin that only one cashier had been cut, an older man who had already been talking about retiring. Maren posted a screenshot of the study's title page and wrote, "so it's not a wave, it's a tide." Mason read it twice. He had spent the day assuming the machines were an ending, and now he was not sure whether he had been pessimistic or merely early, whether the 47 percent was a prophecy or just a measurement of risk, which was a different thing entirely. He typed, deleted, typed again.

In the end he sent only this: "my shift tomorrow is 4 to 9. kiosk side. come by after school if you want, we can test whether the machine knows a cucumber from a zucchini." Marius replied, "bringing the worst produce I can find," and Maren sent the crying-laughing face, and Mason set his alarm, plugged in his phone, and turned off the lamp.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
The season began the way most seasons do, with the smell of cut grass and chain oil and the coach's clipboard slapping against his thigh as he walked the baseline. Ryan had made the team as a sophomore pitcher with a decent curveball and no reputation, and by late April he had both a reputation and a curveball that broke late and hard. He liked the discipline of it, the way practice inculcated the mechanics until his body knew things his mind had never quite learned. He also liked Felicia Amador, who played second base with a violent efficiency he admired, though he had only said about six words to her all season, most of them about the weather.

It happened on a Tuesday, no particular weather at all. A ground ball took a bad hop and she turned her head at the wrong moment and the ball caught her above the ear. She sat down hard on the dirt and Mr. Fischer, who taught chemistry and coached third base, knelt beside her and asked her questions in a low voice while the rest of them stood around the infield doing nothing useful. The athletic trainer arrived with her kit, and Felicia walked off the field under her own power, one hand pressed flat against her skull like she was holding something in.

Ryan learned the protocol from the trainer's laminated sheet, which Felicia kept folded in her back pocket and eventually showed him, because by then they had progressed past the weather. After a concussion, she explained, you came back through graduated steps, starting from total rest and ending at full play, and you only moved to the next step if you stayed free of symptoms. She said it flatly, like reciting the provenance of some document she'd rather not own. Step one was rest, step two was light walking, and she ticked them off with a bitten fingernail. "You can't skip," she said. "You go up one at a time, and if the symptoms come back, you go down."

For three weeks she stood at the fence during practice, and Ryan started arriving early to walk the track with her, because step two was walking and the trainer wanted it done with company. She talked about the headache in a careful, clinical way, as if describing a houseguest whose origins were unclear. She was smarter than he was and read more, and once, discussing the snacks in her bag, she called herself almost epicurean about sunflower seeds, which made him laugh in the gravelly voice he used when he was surprised. In return she laughed at his windup, which she said looked like a man apologizing to a door.

He was on the mound the day she came back for light drills, easy tossing at forty feet, no throwing across the diamond, no diving. He watched her between pitches, and so he saw it happen: she fielded a slow roller, flipped it to the shortstop, and then stopped, put two fingers to her temple, and stood there in the infield dust while everyone else kept moving. The trainer came out again. Ryan heard the conversation later from Felicia, who reported it without drama. The headache had come back during the light drills, so she had to step back a stage, down to the walking, and begin the climb again. She would miss the county tournament, which was two weeks away.

He had thought, before that, in the shallow way he thought about most things, that rules like this were obstacles, red tape between a player and the field. The trainer's protocol had seemed to him a kind of bureaucratic caution, excessive, almost un-American in its patience. But walking the track that evening, while the tournament team took batting practice and the aluminum rang out into the dusk, he found himself turning it over. The slowness was the point. The body announced itself through symptoms, and the protocol was a way of listening. It was the opposite of everything baseball had taught him, which was to pitch through, play through, to treat pain as a negotiable currency, and yet he could not make himself believe the old way anymore. Both ideas sat in him at once, and he could not make them agree.

She watched the tournament from the bench in her warmup jacket, keeping score with the folded protocol beneath the clipboard, and Ryan pitched five innings of the semifinal and lost in the sixth on a ball that Felicia, he was certain, would have caught. Afterward, in the parking lot under the yellow lamps, he told her that, and she looked at the scoreboard for a while.

"I might have," she said. "I also might have gotten another ball off the head and been done for a year." She folded and unfolded the corner of the sheet in her pocket. "I go back to the light drills Monday, if the walking stays clean. Then full practice, then play. I move up only if nothing comes back."

"So you don't know yet," Ryan said.

"No," she said. "I don't know yet." She pulled her cap low against the lamps, picked up her bag, and started across the lot toward her mother's car, cleats clicking on the asphalt the whole way.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
story:
Mya had told everyone she didn't care about missing the math review, and by the time she reached the festival she had almost told herself. The street smelled of fried onions and rose syrup, and her mother was already three stalls ahead, waving at a woman whose name Mya could never remember. It was Eid, technically. It was also four days before the calculus exam, and she had the review sheet folded into her back pocket like evidence.

"I thought Eid was in summer," Liberty said, catching up beside her. Liberty had come because Mya had asked her, which Mya now regretted, because Liberty asked questions the way other people pulled threads. "Like, August. We went to the beach that one time, remember? You had henna all over your hands."

"That was two years ago." Mya kept her eyes on the stall of glass bangles. She knew why, actually. She had looked it up in October, after the exam schedule came out and she'd felt that tectonic lurch of realizing Eid fell on the Wednesday. The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year. She had repeated it to herself like a spell, thinking if she understood the mechanism she could accept the timing. She had not entirely succeeded.

Zain appeared from the crowd carrying a paper boat of biryani, and he gesticulated with his free hand at the stage where the aunties were arguing about the sound system. "Ms. Sharma's here," he said. "She came. She said her class wanted to know about Eid and she figured she should actually see one instead of reading a handout." He paused, spoon in the air. "You look like you're at a funeral."

"I'm fine. I have my notes."

"You said that already," Liberty said. "Twice since the parking lot."

What Liberty wanted, Mya understood slowly and only in pieces, was to be included in a way that didn't require asking. Liberty kept drifting toward the henna stall and drifting back, not requesting anything, waiting to be offered. Mya had been Liberty's plus-one at her cousin's quinceañera in the spring and had felt the same ache, so she recognized it, and still she didn't act on it, because she was busy performing a version of herself that didn't care about the exam. That was the part she couldn't say out loud: not that she minded missing the review, but that she'd pretended not to mind, and the pretending was exhausting her.

Ms. Sharma found them by the mocktail stand. She asked about the food, the prayer that morning, the kids chasing each other with foam swords. Then she said, "Mya, I noticed you're on the list for Wednesday's exam. Is everything alright with the timing?"

"It's fine," Mya said. "It's just a review session."

"Because the school can arrange," Ms. Sharma began, and Mya cut in too fast, saying she'd already worked it out, saying she'd studied ahead in August when Eid was, no, when she'd thought Eid would be far away, saying the words tumbling over each other until Zain said, quietly, "Mya. Sit down for a second."

They sat on the curb behind the stall with the giant pots, where the steam rose and the noise thinned. "It keeps moving," Mya said finally. "That's the thing nobody tells you. Every year it slides back ten or eleven days, and it's not the same day, ever, and you can't plan around it the way other people plan." She heard how it came out, like an accusation, and she didn't fully mean it, or she meant it only halfway. "I looked it up. The calendar's lunar, so it's shorter than the solar one by about ten or eleven days, so everything comes earlier every year. And I thought knowing that would make it feel fair."

"Does it?" Zain asked.

"No. But it makes it feel like a rule instead of a punishment." She laughed, a small unsteady sound. "I keep telling Liberty I don't care about the exam. I care about the exam. I also care about this. Both are true and they're on the same Wednesday and I hate that I keep pretending they're not."

Liberty had followed them without being invited, holding a plate of something she'd bought herself, and Mya saw the plate and understood its meaning. "Come here," Mya said, and pointed at the henna artist's sign. "You've been circling that stall for twenty minutes. Pick a design. My treat, Eid or not."

Ms. Sharma stood at the edge of the curb, waiting until Mya looked up. "So," Ms. Sharma said, "shall I put your name in for the alternate sitting, or shall I not?"

Mya watched Liberty sit down across from the henna artist, extend both palms, and begin, with visible ceremony, to gesticulate at the design book. Somewhere behind them her mother was calling her name.

"Put my name in," Mya said. "I'll be at the review anyway. I'll do both. Somehow I'll do both."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
Lauren had the kitchen table to herself for once, which meant she could spread out everything: the sketchbook, the sharpener, the tin of pencils she had dumped sideways so the grades faced her like a jury.
