The portfolio deadline was in eleven days, and the drawing she wanted to submit, a portrait of her grandmother from an old photograph, kept ruining itself. Every time she shaded the cheekbones, her hand dragged through the graphite and smeared it into a gray haze, as if the face were dissolving in weather.

Her mother passed through to the sink with a colander of grapes and paused long enough to say it looked like the woman in the photo had been caught in a sandstorm. "That's the smudge problem," Lauren said, not looking up. "I'm solving it." Her mother said the grapes were for fermenting into something a coworker had promised was easy, and left Lauren to wonder how a person could ferment grapes and still describe any part of it as easy.

The doorbell rang before she could get angry at the paper. Marshall stood on the mat holding a grocery bag of licorice and, as usual, talking before she had fully opened the door. He was the most garrulous person in her grade, which was useful when you wanted the entire history of a substitute teacher by lunch and exhausting at all other times. He said he'd come to see the doomed portrait, because Rayden had told him it looked like the woman was standing behind frosted glass, and Rayden was not a person who exaggerated, being constitutionally incapable of adjectives.

He sat down across from her, unwound a strand of licorice, and looked at the smeared cheekbone for a long, quiet minute, which for Marshall was practically monastic. "Which grade did you use?" he asked. Lauren turned the pencil to show him the stamped letter. "This one. It says 6B."

"Okay, so here's the thing my uncle told me when he was showing me his drafting kit. The core of a pencil is a mix of graphite and clay. More clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, and those are marked H. Less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B." He pointed at the 6B. "You're drawing with basically the softest, darkest one in your tin. It's clay-starved. It wants to smudge. You've given it no choice."

Lauren looked at the pencil as if meeting someone she'd misjudged. She dug through the tin and found a 2H, its point still needle-sharp because she never used it, and drew one test stroke on the corner of the page. The line came out pale and crisp and did not move when she dragged her thumb across it. She tried a 4B next to it, softer and darker, and it ghosted slightly under her thumb but held its shape better than the 6B had. The pencil companies had graded them and she had never once thought about what the grades were grading.

So she started the cheekbones again, and here was where her two ideas about the drawing had to argue with each other. Ms. Sinclair, in the one portfolio workshop Lauren had attended, had told her that her best work had "commitment in the darks," that she shouldn't be afraid of a deep black. But commitment in the darks, Lauren now understood, was exactly what had been melting her grandmother's face. The softer pencils gave the richest darks and smudged the most; the harder ones behaved and stayed pale. She couldn't have both from one stick of graphite and clay. She laid in the structure with the 2H, built the middle tones with the 4B, and saved the 6B for only the deepest shadows under the jaw, pressing once and then refusing to let her hand cross that ground again.

It worked, mostly. The face stopped dissolving. But there was a softness in the original smudge that she found herself missing, a kind of breath around the edges that the disciplined strokes didn't have, and she hadn't decided yet whether that was a real loss or just the appeal of a mistake she'd gotten attached to. When she said this out loud, Marshall pronounced it the wisest thing she'd ever said about art, which she distrusted, since he also called a vending machine "wise" when it gave him two bags of chips.

"You know what's funny," he said, rolling a licorice wheel to the edge of the table and losing interest in it. "You've got, like, fifteen pencils, and the difference between them is just clay. You've been treating them as one thing your whole life. They were never one thing." Lauren said that was either profound or a comment about how much he talked, and he said both could be true, which was the kind of answer he gave when he wanted to seem to have sagacity, though this once she let him have it.

The kitchen had gone dusky without her noticing. Her mother came back through with a jar of grapes that were allegedly becoming something and set it on the counter behind them. Lauren picked up the 2H and, in the corner of the page where the test strokes lived, wrote the date and then, underneath, in letters so light you'd have to tilt the paper toward the window to read them, "more clay, more control." She looked at it for a moment, crossed nothing out, and turned back to the portrait's left eye.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: In hockey, a saucer pass lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over an opponent's stick and lands on the receiver's blade.
story:
The problem had been waiting for Adam all week, written on the clipboard he carried but could not solve: the under-twelves he coached kept losing the ball in the middle third, because every pass they played along the ground ran straight into a defender's outstretched foot. He had tried cones, tried shouting "earlier, earlier," tried making them pass two-touch. Nothing held. On Saturday morning he stood at the halfway line of the field behind the school, twenty-two kids in yellow bibs scattered around him, and realized he had no drill for what was wrong with them.

"Again," he called, and watched the same thing happen. Kalen received with his back turned, spun, and rolled the ball flat toward the left wing, where a small boy named Thabo was marking the space. The defender slid a foot out, and the move died. Kalen put his hands on his knees. Adam blew the whistle mostly to have something to do with his hands.

That evening he went to Martin's house, where the plan had been video games and had become, without anyone deciding it, watching hockey highlights on Martin's laptop. In one clip a player slid the puck sideways and it rose, briefly, just off the ice, sailed over a sprawled defender's stick, and settled neatly onto a teammate's blade without a bounce.

"What was that," Adam said, leaning in. He made Martin replay it three times.

"It's called a saucer pass," Martin said. "It lifts the puck just off the ice so it flies flat over the other guy's stick and lands right on the receiver's blade."

"Flat," Adam repeated. He was already not entirely in the room. He was on a soccer field, thinking about feet instead of sticks, about a ball instead of a puck, about whether the same idea could survive the translation. Martin talked on about the player's stick angle, and Adam half-listened, because in his head he was watching Thabo's foot slide out and imagining the ball going up and over it, then down, then rolling on.

Later, at his desk, he wrote to Kalen, because Kalen had played since he was five and would tell him the truth.

Hey. Crazy question. If the little kids chipped their passes just over the defenders' feet instead of playing everything on the ground, does that work in soccer or does it just slow everything down? Every pass through the middle is getting cut out and I'm out of ideas.

Kalen's reply came while Adam was still staring at his own message, worried it portended another week of blocked passes and long faces. "It works if it's small. Little chip, barely off the ground, comes down rolling. Big lofted one and someone will head it away while your guy is still watching it." Then a second message: "You'd have to teach them the weight though. That's the hard part."

The hard part turned out to be exactly that. On Monday Adam set out two low hurdles in the middle third, about a meter apart, and told the kids the hurdles were defenders' feet. Pass over the foot, land before your teammate, arrive rolling. The first ten minutes were a comedy of balls ballooning into the next field, and one boy, Sipho, developed a look of such wounded concentration that Adam had to turn away to keep from laughing. But he kept his instructions small, no speeches, just "lower" and "softer," and by the end of the session Thabo clipped one over the first hurdle that dropped flat and ran into Kalen's little brother's path like a pass on rails. Kalen's brother didn't even break stride. He just took it and went.

Ms. Mokoena, who taught math and watched the Saturday sessions from the bleachers with her coffee, caught Adam gathering the hurdles afterward. "That looked different today," she said. "Whatever you changed, keep it."

"It's a hockey thing," Adam said. "Sort of. Half a hockey thing." He stacked the hurdles in the shed and thought about telling her the whole route, the highlight clip, the message to Kalen, the two hours he had spent on the porch chipping a ball over his mother's watering can to feel the weight in his ankle. He didn't. Some of it he was still unsure of anyway: whether the chip would survive against real defenders who jumped, whether Sipho would ever trust it, whether he had taught them something or only staged a version of something. He knew what had worked today. He did not yet know if it would work Saturday.

Saturday came, and with it a friendly against a school from across town whose defenders were bigger and faster and, in the opening minutes, played with something close to malevolent patience. Twice in the first five minutes the middle third closed like a drawer. Adam stood on the touchline with his hands in his pockets and did not shout, though every platitude he owned rose in him, "want it more," "keep your heads up," phrases that meant nothing and cost nothing to say.

Then Kalen's brother received with his back to goal, felt the pressure come, and without looking up clipped the ball over a sliding foot. It dipped, landed rolling, and Thabo ran onto it at full stride.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769, using knowledge from his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain.
story:
Olivier spread the maps across his grandfather's kitchen table, which was the only surface in the house not already holding something. The house smelled of coffee and the sea, the latter being unavoidable in a town where the water came to the edge of the garden and made its opinions known. Tomorrow morning he had to stand up in Ms. Traoré's class and explain how a current off the American coast kept northern Europe warmer than it had any right to be, and at the moment he could not have explained how the kettle worked.

"You're doing this here?" his grandfather said, setting down two mugs. "In my kitchen. Where I eat."

"You said come any time. Theresa and Kaydence are meeting me at nine to practice. We're presenting together."

"I said come any time," his grandfather agreed, in the tone of a man revising a contract. He wanted Olivier's help relighting the boiler before dark, Olivier suspected, or possibly he simply wanted company and would have demurred, sincerely and to the end, if accused of it. Instead he leaned over the table and tapped the Atlantic map with one finger. "What's this snake doing here?"

"The Gulf Stream. It's warm water moving north along the coast, then east. Ms. Traoré says it's why Britain and Norway aren't as cold as Canada at the same latitude, and I have to say why, out loud, for three minutes, without reading off the card." Olivier turned the current map over, then back, as if the reverse might be easier. The arrows were color-coded, orange for warm, blue for cold, and the whole system looked less like a river and more like weather drawn by someone with a grudge.

His grandfather studied it longer than a bored man would have. "You know who put that current on a chart first?"

"Ms. Traoré mentioned somebody. Some scientist." Olivier reached for his notebook, where he had written "Franklin? 1700s? London?" and then, underneath, a note to himself that said "CHECK THIS," which he had not done.

"Benjamin Franklin. He had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769." His grandfather said it the way he reported tide times, as information the world had no excuse not to know. "But he didn't figure it out from measuring. His cousin was a whaling captain out of Nantucket, Timothy Folger. Folger knew the current from working it, and the captains were already steering around it to save days, going to London. Franklin drew what the sailors knew."

Olivier stopped writing. "Wait. The ship captains knew before the scientists?"

"Ships have to arrive. That concentrates the mind." His grandfather straightened up, wincing at whatever his back had to say about the motion. "That's your three minutes, right there. The chart is the interesting part."

It was, and Olivier resented that it was, because he had planned to talk about temperature gradients and had already made a diagram with colored pencils, and colored pencils were hard to walk away from. He texted Theresa: did she know about the captain. She wrote back a single line of vitriolic capitals, to the effect that she had spent her evening on latitude comparisons and nobody had mentioned any captain. Kaydence sent a shrugging emoji and then, in a separate message, "bring the maps."

At nine they came, Theresa carrying her laptop like evidence for a trial and Kaydence carrying, inexplicably, a bag of clementines. They arranged themselves around the table, displacing the grandfather, who took his mug to the armchair by the window and made a show of reading a newspaper that was three days old. He wanted to stay. Olivier understood this perfectly and said nothing, because saying something would have spoiled it.

Theresa's half of the presentation was rigorous and slightly joyless, a comparison of average January temperatures between coastal Norway and inland Canada at the same latitude, delivered in the flat voice she used for things she intended to be unarguable. Kaydence had drawn the class a comic. Olivier had the map, the arrows, and now, borrowed without attribution, the story of the chart. He practiced it twice: warm water, eastern shore, bends east across the Atlantic, northern Europe warmer than the latitude deserves. Then the twist, the part that had reorganized his whole understanding of the assignment: that a current could be known, used, and avoided for years before anyone drew it, and that the drawing came from a printer in London but the knowledge came from a cousin on a whaleship.

"Do you believe that?" Theresa said. "That nobody had charted it before?"

"I believe the printing part. 1769, London, that's the fact. Whether the captains were the first people ever to notice warm water, I don't know." He looked at the map again. "I can't prove a negative. Nobody noticed it in writing, as far as I know, and as far as I know isn't very far."

"So you'll say that? Out loud? To Ms. Traoré?"

"She likes when people say what they don't know. She says it's the difference between a student and a parrot." Kaydence peeled a clementine in one long spiral, which was somehow the most confident thing anyone had done all evening.

The presentation went fine, which is to say nothing catastrophic occurred before nine-fifteen the next morning, when Olivier stood at the front of Ms. Traoré's room with the map blu-tacked to the board and said the words he had decided on the night before: warm current, eastern seaboard, bends east, northern Europe warmer than its latitude owes it, and then the chart, London, 1769, the captain cousin, the ships saving days. He said, "What we can't know is who noticed it first, because noticing doesn't leave a record," and Ms. Traoré wrote something on her clipboard that he could not read, which was probably the point of clipboards.

That afternoon he went back to his grandfather's house, ostensibly to finish relighting the boiler, which had been their agreed arrangement all along and which his grandfather had not once mentioned. On the kitchen table, weighted down with the sugar bowl, lay a photocopy of an old chart: the Atlantic, the coastline, and a long raised line of marks running northeast like a spine, with a title in faded capitals. His grandfather was at the stove, not turning around.

"Found that in a drawer," he said. "Thought your class might like to see what they were steering around."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.
story:
Jordan's father had left the car keys on the kitchen table beside a folded note, and the note was the first test of the morning. "Back at six," it read. "Your uncle says you learn by ruining the clutch. Please learn gently. Love, Dad." Jordan pocketed the keys, ate half a piece of toast, and stood for a while at the front window looking at the slope of Emerson Street, which fell away from their house in one long, patient grade toward the stop sign. He had passed everything on the practice test except the parking. The parking was a language he did not yet speak.

Cristian arrived at nine on his bike, helmet still buckled, like a man who took no chances with anything except his own opinions. "You're doing it on the hill?" he said. "Nobody does it on the hill." Jordan said the hill was the only place to do it, because the test route ran past the school and the school sat on the hill, and if the examiner asked him to park there, he would have to park there, gravity included. Cristian considered this with the expression of someone being asked to admire a flaw. "Fine," he said. "But if you roll into Mrs. Okafor's hedge, I'm telling everyone it was my idea."

They set out two recycling bins as the imaginary car ahead and a basketball as the imaginary car behind, and Jordan began the slow arithmetic of it all. Reverse, angle, straighten, watch the curb. The first attempt put him two feet out and Cristian rated it, generously, as a parking attempt. The second kissed the curb with the rear tire and left the front swung wide like a dog pointing at something. By the fifth, something shifted, the way handwriting shifts when you stop thinking about the letters. He was in. Tight, straight, parallel. He sat with his hands on the wheel and felt the car settle against its own brakes, and only then did he notice, really notice, that the whole street was downhill, and the car was a held breath.

His phone buzzed against the cup holder. Sarah-Maude, who had taken her test in April and spoke of it the way veterans speak of winters: "How's the parking going? Also my dad says remind your dad about the indemnity clause, whatever that is, apparently it matters if you scratch the car. Also: slopes. Did you do the wheels?" Jordan read it twice. The wheels. He looked down through the driver's window at his front tires, which pointed straight ahead, aimed down the hill like they had somewhere to be.

He texted back: "What about the wheels?" and her reply came in three instalments, the way her thoughts always did. "Facing downhill next to a curb you turn them toward the curb." Then: "Toward the curb means the car rolls into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail." Then, because she could never leave anything unadorned: "Not that brakes fail. But still. Wheels." Jordan turned the key a quarter so the wheel unlocked, spun the front tires toward the curb, and sat looking at them. The curb was six inches away, an ordinary strip of concrete, and suddenly it was a whole idea.

Mr. Tehrani, from three doors down, was watering his mums in defiance of the hour and the heat, and he wandered over with the hose still dribbling. "Parallel park," he observed. "Which way are the wheels?" Jordan told him, and Mr. Tehrani nodded slowly, twice, the way he did when a boy had answered something a boy usually got wrong. "Most people say away," he said. "They think the car should be ready to leave. But the curb is not for leaving. The curb is for catching." Cristian, sprawled on the basketball, said, "Mr. Tehrani, if the brakes fail and Jordan dies on Emerson Street, is his dad's insurance going to pay for the hedge or the funeral first?" Mr. Tehrani said he imagined the hedge, and Jordan laughed so suddenly he had to put the car in park.

The highway was the afternoon's country. His father came home early, changed his shirt, and took him out to the loop where the on-ramp fed into three lanes of traffic moving like weather. His father's method was silence, mostly, punctuated by small meteorology: "Truck." "Blind spot." "Faster, love, this isn't a museum." Merging, Jordan discovered, was the opposite of parking. Parking was about shrinking, about negotiating with a fixed world; merging was about joining a moving one, matching its speed and its gaps, acclimating to the current until the current stopped being a current and became just the road. He wondered which one a life was more like, and whether the answer changed depending on the year, and he didn't say any of this out loud because his father was saying "Signal" in the tone of a man reminding a surgeon of the time.

On the way home his father had him park on the hill, in front of the recycling bins, one last full rehearsal. Jordan slid in on the first try, clean, and reached for the key, and then paused, and turned the wheel toward the curb, and let the tires rest there. His father watched him do it and said nothing, which from his father was applause.

That night Cristian texted a photograph of the basketball, still lying in the gutter where he had left it, with the caption "the other car, waiting for you." Jordan lay on his bed with the window open, listening to Emerson Street hold its long slope in the dark, and thought about wheels that point into the thing that stops you. Tomorrow he'd practise the three-point turn. He typed back, "Tell the other car I'm coming," and turned off the lamp.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In England, the Tenant Fees Act 2019 caps most tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under £50,000.
story:
The email arrived at 4:12 on a Thursday, and by 4:20 Maelle was on the bus to Kendra's flat with her phone in her fist like a verdict. The landlord's message said the deposit for the studio would be two months' rent, payable by Friday noon, or he would offer the place to the next person on the list. Two months. Maelle had done the arithmetic four times on the rattling bus window, and each time the number came out larger than the money she had.

Kendra's mum let her in with a look that said she understood everything already. Kendra was at the kitchen table with Baby, who was eating cereal out of a mug because, she claimed, all the bowls were "emotionally compromised." They had planned a revision evening for their history exam, which was Monday, and which none of them had started, and which was now the smaller of several problems.

"Two months," Maelle said, dropping her bag. "Nine hundred a month, so eighteen hundred. I have twelve hundred. My gran gave me the twelve hundred. It took her two years."

Baby peered into her mug as though the answer might be at the bottom. "So borrow six hundred from somewhere."

"From where? The Bank of Baby?"

"The Bank of Baby charges interest in crisps," Baby said, "but its reserves are low."

Kendra spun her phone across the table. "Wait. Is he even allowed to ask for that?" She had gone pale, which for Kendra meant she had remembered something. Her family had moved three times in four years, and she had habituated herself to the vocabulary of letting agents the way other people habituated themselves to weather. "My mum used to go on about it. There was a law or something. Caps on deposits."

Maelle's first instinct was to dismiss this as one of Kendra's half-remembered certainty, the kind that had once convinced them all that Henry VIII had six wives executed. But the claim had the shape of a real thing, so she typed it out, keyword by keyword, while Baby narrated over her shoulder. Deposit caps. Tenant fees. England. The results assembled themselves on the screen, and Maelle read them twice, because the first time she didn't believe her luck.

"The Tenant Fees Act 2019," she read. "It caps most tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds."

Baby counted on her fingers, then recounted, then looked up with the expression of someone who had solved a crime. "Five weeks. Nine hundred a month is about two hundred and seven a week. Five weeks is just over a thousand."

"A thousand and thirty-five," Maelle said. Her voice came out strange, half triumph and half fury, because the triumph and the fury were about the same fact. He had asked for eighteen hundred. He was allowed a bit over a thousand. She had almost emptied her gran's gift to overpay a man who surely knew the rules, and the knowledge sat in her chest like something swallowed too fast.

She typed the reply on the walk to the letting agent's office, Kendra and Baby trailing her like a legal team that had done no coursework. She kept the message short and factual, quoting the cap, quoting five weeks, quoting the fifty thousand, and asking him to confirm the corrected figure by noon Friday. Then she stood outside the office window watching a man in a shiny tie explain something to a young couple, and she thought that the whole city was a substrate on which this one law lay printed invisibly, that people moved across it daily without knowing it was there, the way she had until twenty minutes ago. Her specious plan to borrow from a payday lender, formed somewhere around the third bus stop and abandoned by the fourth, now struck her as so obviously rotten that she almost laughed at her earlier self.

The reply came at 9:41 that night, while the three of them ate toast over their history notes in Kendra's kitchen. "Apologies, an oversight on our part. Corrected deposit: £1,035. Contract available for signature tomorrow by noon." Kendra's mum put her head round the door at the sound of their cheering and said, "What did you three actually revise," and none of them could answer.

Maelle signed the next morning in an office that smelled of carpet cleaner. The agent was pleasant and brisk and did not meet her eyes for quite as long as she would have liked. Outside, on the pavement, she transferred the deposit from her gran's gift and watched the balance drop, and the studio was hers from the first of the month, and she still had money left over, and none of it changed the fact that she had needed a law to protect her from an adult who had smiled at her through that same window two days before. She texted her gran a photo of the keys she would collect Monday, right after the history exam she had now definitively not revised for.

"Five weeks," Baby had said that morning, holding up her hand with all fingers spread. "The whole thing, in a hand."

"Shut up and test me on the Reformation," Maelle said, and Baby grinned and opened the textbook.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.
story:
The deadline for the portfolio was three weeks away, and William had ten half-finished paintings spread across two tables in the art room, none of them speaking to the others. He had chosen his theme back in September, or thought he had, and the theme was drowning. Everything he painted after that was water in some form: a flooded parking garage, his grandmother's kitchen sink overflowing, a boy standing waist-deep in a lake with his hands in his pockets. But the paintings looked like ten different artists had made them, and the artist's statement, the one page Mr. Banerjee required, had been drafted eleven times and deleted eleven times.

"The artist intends to explore the theme of water as memory," William read aloud from his twelfth attempt, sitting on the counter beside the drying rack while Avah sorted brushes into jars behind him.

"Who's the artist?" Avah asked, not looking up. "You're the artist. You painted them."

"That's how you write these things. Formally." He heard how thin it sounded. Mr. Banerjee had circled the phrase "the artist" in his last draft with red pen and written a single word in the margin: coward.

Richard came in with his camera bag, dropped it on a stool, and leaned over the flooded garage painting. "This one's the best. It's the only one where you don't know what's going to happen." Richard was applying to film school and had, all autumn, a way of talking about images as if they were evidence of a crime. "The others are all resolved. You already decided what they mean before you painted them."

William wanted to argue, but the argument wasn't there. He looked at the lake painting, the boy with hands in pockets, and it was true that he had known exactly what that painting meant when he started it, which was maybe why it felt dead. He thought of his father, who worked at a bank and spoke at dinner about fiduciary duty as if it were a religion, who believed that if you took someone's money you owed them certainty. His father wanted him to apply to business school. There was a version of William's father inside William too, the part that wanted every painting to pay off, to be explicable, to say what it had been hired to say.

In October, before any of this, Mr. Banerjee had kept him after class. "You're not making images," he had said, sitting on the edge of the desk with his sleeves rolled up. "You're making illustrations of sentences." William had bristled at that, and Mr. Banerjee had seen him bristle and softened, which somehow made it worse. "Pick something you can't finish thinking about," he had said. "Then the portfolio will have a reason to exist." That was the night William had started the drowning paintings, though he'd told everyone, and half believed, that the theme was about water.

Avah set down the jar of brushes and came to read over his shoulder. "It says here the artist uses oil because of its slow drying time. Do you?"

"I use acrylic. I copied that sentence from a statement online."

"So write what you actually do. And say I. An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist. That's the whole point. It's yours." She tapped the page. "You keep hiding behind 'the artist' like he's some third guy who's going to take the blame."

William laughed despite himself, and something in the laugh loosened the afternoon. He pulled out a fresh sheet of paper and wrote, without drafting, "I am afraid of water. I learned to swim at nine and I have never liked it. I paint floods because I want to look at the thing slowly and from a distance, which is also how I look at everything else." The pen stopped. He read the sentences back and felt exposed in a way that the paintings, for all their water, had never made him feel. The paintings were a screen. The page was a window, and he had just opened it.

"That's the real one," Richard said, reading upside down from across the table. "It's also kind of anachronistic, honestly. Nobody under forty writes like that. It sounds like a letter."

"Maybe I want it to sound like a letter."

"Then you have to decide that on purpose." Richard swung his camera up and took a photograph of William sitting there with the paper, unasked, the flash popping once against the grey window light. "For my portfolio. Contradiction. A guy who paints drowning surrounded by a room full of his own water and looking completely dry."

William spent the last hour before the building closed choosing which four paintings to cut. It hurt more than he expected; the lake painting with the boy's hands in his pockets went first, then the sink, then two he'd been privately proud of. Ten became six, and Mr. Banerjee required ten, which meant four new works in three weeks, in a medium he could barely afford, on a subject he had just admitted frightened him in writing. He stacked the survivors against the wall and slid the rejects into the flat file drawer where the unfinished things went to be forgotten. His father would say the trade was bad: certainty for confession, a business degree for six paintings of floodwater and a page of first person.

At the door, Avah asked whether he regretted writing it that way. William zipped his bag and looked back at the six paintings leaning in a row, and at the drawer holding the other four.

"Ask me in three weeks," he said, and turned off the lights.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
The cones were still in Laura's garage from her own playing days, back when the coach used to stop every drill to correct her, and the smell of the rubber when she dumped them onto the grass made her fourteen again for a second, standing in the cold while a voice told her to bend her wrist. Now she was the one setting up at Riverside Park for ten eleven-year-olds who could not complete a pass to save their lives. The coach, her old coach, had handed her the clipboard on Tuesday and said, "They're weak in passing. Fix it."

She had spent two nights designing drills, and every one of them was built on instructions like the ones she remembered receiving: lock your ankle, follow through, keep your hips square to the target. The kids nodded and did none of it. Their passes skidded into gutters of dead grass, rolled out at the knees of receivers who had stopped expecting anything.

"You're teaching them like we got taught," Tanisha said from the bench, where she was supposed to be helping but was mostly peeling an orange. "Remember how much that helped you?"

"It helped some," Laura said, though she was not sure that was true. She remembered mostly the freezing, the stopping, the feeling of her own body becoming a list of broken parts. She had quit at fifteen. She had told everyone it was schoolwork.

The kids came back from the water fountain and Laura lined them up for the gate drill again, ten passes through the cones to Bryden, who was standing in as target because he had wandered over from the basketball courts and found it funny. "Bryden," she called, "hold your hands out where you want the ball." And the first kid, without being told anything about her ankle or her hips, looked at Bryden's hands and hit them.

Laura stood very still on the touchline. The second kid did the same. The third bounced it short, and Laura almost said "open your foot," but instead she said, "Hit his hands, not his shins," and the fourth pass was flat and true and Bryden had to jump to catch it.

"What just happened?" Tanisha said, coming over with her orange.

"I have no idea," Laura said, and she meant it in the best way. She tried it again on the other wing, then with moving targets, and it kept happening: tell them where the ball should go and they improved; tell them what their bodies should do and they stiffened and failed. She had a memory then, sharp as a stud on bare skin, of being told in her last season that she overthought everything, and of thinking, at the time, that this was an insult rather than a diagnosis of the coaching itself.

That night she looked it up and found a researcher named Gabriele Wulf, whose studies showed that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, like the target, rather than on their own body parts. It was not a secret, exactly. It was sitting in plain sight, and nobody had ever told her, or the man who coached her, or the man who coached that man. An entire tradition of instruction, passed down because it had always been passed down, obsolescent and still standing, like the old wooden bleachers behind the far goal that no one had removed since the new ones were built. She read the sentence twice. She had spent years thinking the problem was her wrists.

By Thursday she had rewritten every drill. The cones became gates marked with bright tape so the kids had a target to see, and she made the smallest kid, who usually stood at the edge chewing his sleeve, the designated receiver everyone had to hit. "You're making him the whole game," Bryden said from the fence, where he now showed up without being asked.

"Maybe," Laura said. She was aware of a pressure she could not fully name, the feeling that if she let herself believe she had found something true, she would also have to look straight at what had been done to her, and at how easily she had done it to others in her very first week. Tanisha had once called their old team an oligarchy, three senior girls deciding everything, and Laura had laughed and not disagreed, which was its own kind of agreeing.

The last drill of the evening was a passing pattern, and it fell apart in the new way, chaotically and loudly, the kids arguing about whose fault, the smallest boy near tears because he had missed twice. Laura gathered them in and said, "Eyes on the hands you're throwing to. That's all. The hands." And they ran it again, and it was beautiful for about forty seconds, and then the smallest boy kicked the ball over the fence and into the duck pond, and they all stood watching it float.

"I'll get it," he said, and he climbed the fence, and the others cheered him like a hero, and Laura did not stop them, and out on the water the ball drifted slowly toward the far bank where she could not follow it.

"So," Tanisha said beside her, peeling another orange. "You going to coach next year, or are you going to play?"

Laura watched the boy's sneakers sink into the mud. "I used to think I quit because I wasn't good enough," she said.

"And now?"

"Now I think I quit because every time I got the ball, I heard a list." A pair of mallards were investigating the ball, nudging it toward the reeds. "I don't know yet which one of those is the real reason. Maybe both. Maybe I'll figure it out on the way to the pond."

She climbed the fence.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
Ms. Xu had written one sentence on the board before the bell finished ringing, and Brody copied it into his notebook before he had any idea what it meant: "In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages." Underneath it she had drawn two columns and written "Satis House" at the top of a list of characters from Great Expectations that the class would spend the period sorting.

"Owners on the left," she said. "Workers on the right. Persuade me."

Tiffany claimed the marker first, because Tiffany wanted the presentation grade that came with running the board, and she had told Brody at lunch that she needed an A in this class for her scholarship application. She wrote Miss Havisham in the left column without hesitating. Then she paused over Joe Gargery, marker hovering, and the room drifted into the somnolence that came with any discussion that started before ten in the morning.

"She doesn't do anything," Myles said from the back. "Miss Havisham just sits in her wedding dress. How is she an owner?"

"She owns the house," Brody said. "The brewery too, even shut down. That's the whole point of the sentence. Look at it again." He read it out loud, slowly, and something rearranged itself in his head as he did. "It's not about working. She never has to work. The house and the land make her the bourgeoisie, and the people who have to sell their labour to live are the proletariat."

Tiffany wrote Joe on the right, then Magwitch, then Pip, and then stopped again. "Pip gets money halfway through," she said. "He has his expectations."

"He has an allowance," Brody said. "Somebody else is still pulling it out of a factory somewhere. Magwitch, actually. Magwitch extrudes the money out of the colonies and pipes it to Pip, and Pip spends his life being ashamed of the man doing the producing." He had not planned to say that; it came out whole, and Myles sat up as though Brody had elbowed him.

"That's your essay," Myles said. "That's literally your thesis right there."

But Brody was already doubting it, because Pip's ambition was the thing he had loved about the book when he read it alone in August, before anyone taught him to be suspicious of it. He wanted Estella and London and a life where his hands stayed clean. Brody had spent the summer filling out forms for a college his father had not gone to, and he understood wanting to be a different kind of person so exactly that it frightened him. If the Marxist reading was right, then the thing Pip wanted was a lie sold to keep him compliant, and the thing Brody wanted might be the same lie, wearing newer clothes.

He said none of this aloud. Instead he raised his hand, and when Ms. Xu nodded at him, he asked whether a person could be both. "Pip works for a while, as an apprentice, and then he lives off Magwitch's money. Estella is property herself, sort of, raised to be given away. Where do you put her?"

Ms. Xu smiled the way she did when a question was better than an answer. "Put her where you can defend," she said, which was her way of refusing to decide for them, and Brody felt the small humiliation and the larger relief of it at once.

Tiffany solved her own problem in the last ten minutes. She ruled a third column down the middle of the board, labelled it "in motion," and placed Pip's name in it with an arrow from right to left and a question mark where the arrow ended. "That's the presentation," she announced, and Ms. Xu wrote something in her book that made Tiffany exhale. When the bell rang, Myles gathered his bag slowly, waiting until the room cleared, and then said, "So when you write it, are you going to say the ambition is fake?"

"I don't know yet," Brody said. "I think I'm going to say he's between the columns, and so am I." He looked at the whiteboard, at his own name nowhere on it, at the arrow ending in nothing, and then he copied the third column into his notes exactly as Tiffany had drawn it.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
His father had set the ballot flyer beside the salt, as if registration were a dish that could be passed. James pushed his peas around and said, "I turned in the form at the post office today." His mother asked which party he leaned toward, and his grandmother, visiting from Ottawa, looked up from her plate with an interest she usually saved for dessert.

"I'll be eighteen in March," James said. "Before the election." He felt the weight of saying it out loud, like admitting he had signed something binding. "It's weird. Kathy's dad drives her to vote like it's a chore, and Yaseen says his family argues about it every night and then all vote the same way anyway."

His grandmother put down her fork. "You know it wasn't always eighteen," she said. "Canada lowered the federal voting age from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970." She said it simply, the way she recited phone numbers.

James did the arithmetic without wanting to. "So before that, someone my age couldn't." He thought of Yaseen, who had given a scathing speech in Ms. Whitehead's class about lowering the voting age to sixteen, calling it a publicity stunt, and of Kathy, who had countered that same afternoon that sixteen-year-olds pay taxes on their paycheques. James had stayed quiet in that room, agreeing with whichever one spoke last. "How old were you, in 1970?"

"Twenty-two. It changed the year after my first vote." She smiled, but there was something wistful in it. "My brother missed two elections waiting to turn twenty-one. He used to say the politicians who sent boys to war weren't the ones those boys could vote against."

The table went quiet the way it did when his grandmother accidentally opened a door to something historical. His father refilled the water glasses. James kept thinking about the arithmetic, how recently the line had moved, how a line that moves once might move again, or might never move at all. He had told Ms. Whitehead after class that he hadn't decided which side he was on, and she had said, "Undecided isn't the same as unthinking," which he'd carried home like a permission slip.

Later, drying dishes while his mother washed, he texted Yaseen: did you know it was 21 until 1970. Three dots appeared, stopped, appeared again. Yaseen replied that his uncle had mentioned it once, and that it had changed his speech, maybe, or ought to. Then a second message: "so would you have voted at 16?" James stood with the towel in his hands, the window over the sink showing the dark street and his own reflection holding a phone. He typed, deleted, and typed again: "honestly I don't know yet." Above the sink his grandmother's coat hung on the hook by the door, and from the living room came the sound of her laughing at something on television, a person who had outlived one rule about who counted and was watching to see what the next one would be. He set the phone face down on the counter and picked up the last plate.
